articles.title_orig: John Ross: What’s behind the positive Xi–Trump summit?
articles.title_zh: John Ross: What’s behind the positive Xi–Trump summit?
articles.content_orig:
In a recent interview on India & Global Left , British economist John Ross, senior fellow at the Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies at Renmin University of China, discusses the significance of Xi Jinping’s state visit to the United States. In his view, the summit was positive mainly for what did not happen: Washington launched no new attack on China. The relative stability between the two countries reflects not goodwill but China’s strength – after Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs ran into China’s counter-measures on rare earths, the US switched to going after other targets.
That approach, John argues, has largely failed. The attempted “reverse Kissinger” to detach Russia from China has gone nowhere; Cuba has not buckled under the oil blockade; and in the war on Iran, “this is a fifteen-round contest and we’re probably up to about round five – but so far Iran’s won all five of the rounds.”
He characterises the New Cold War as, to an extent, the reverse of the first one. The Soviet Union was a military equal of the US but never an economic one, so Washington shifted the contest onto economic terrain. Today China is outgrowing the US and leading in EVs, batteries, drones, biotech and parts of AI, so the US seeks to shift the contest onto military terrain – hence the encouragement of German and Japanese rearmament, the military pressure on Venezuela, Cuba and Iran, and the attempts to stir up trouble in the South China Sea.
The interview also covers the security picture in East Asia, Europe’s self-defeating subordination to Washington, and why the Global South will keep trading with China regardless.
John will be among the speakers at the Socialist China Conference in London on Saturday 3 October. Tickets are available on Eventbrite .
The interview was first broadcast on India & Global Left . The transcript below is AI-generated.
Host: Hello and welcome to another episode of India and Global Left . If you’re new to the show, please hit that subscribe button. Also consider becoming a YouTube member, a Patreon, or donating a small amount via the link in the description box. Without further ado, let me welcome our guest tonight, John Ross. John is a British economist and he is known for his academic work on China. He’s a senior fellow at the Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies, Renmin University of China. John, welcome back to India and Global Left .
John Ross: Very pleased to be here.
Host: I want to discuss with you the US–China relationship in general, and I thought the recent summit in the United States of America between China and the US is interesting. The Chinese media’s coverage has been, broadly speaking, very positive. I wonder what is your analysis about the significance of the summit?
John Ross: Well, I think the estimate from the Chinese media — positive — is correct, in the following sense: that the United States did not launch any big attacks on China. In fact, from the point of substantial agreement, not many things came out of the meeting.
One interesting detail was that the tariff truce was only extended until January, when it was widely reported — I’m not saying it was true, but it was widely reported, and it would obviously be in China’s interests to extend it for a longer period of time — what was reported in the press was until the end of the Trump presidency. That means it leaves the US with room for manoeuvre, because China’s not going to launch a tariff offensive against the US, but the US may against China.
If we look at what’s behind this, I think it’s the fact that the United States found out that China is a very strong opponent, and therefore, for tactical reasons due to the international situation at the moment, the US genuinely does not want at this particular moment in time to have a confrontation with China. And to explain why — or Trump doesn’t, let’s put it more precisely, because there are people in the US who do, but let’s talk about Trump.
If we call the first Trump presidency Trump 1.0: he decided, together with the general establishment view that China is the main enemy — which remains the view of all serious foreign policy circles within the United States — and he launched a frontal attack on it. This did not go well. It didn’t have any significant effect at all on China’s economy. China didn’t change its policies. Actually, many people in the US thought this was a very foolish policy. I mean, it’s not very sensible to attack your enemy’s strongest point; a military commander would not give that as the advice they’d give.
Biden then didn’t reverse the things which Trump did, and in the technology field he added some. And Trump, when he came to Trump 2.0, made an attempt to attack China in the so-called Liberation Day tariffs, which ended up with the tariffs against China being at 145% — which basically means no trade would take place at that level of tariffs.
And China, as in usual China style, didn’t make very big noise, but it just struck back. It struck back with its own tariffs, and in particular it struck back with rare earths. And the American military said to Trump, “We can’t produce military equipment without the rare earths from China.” The American motor industry said to Trump, “We’ll have to close down in about six months without the rare earths from China.” And Trump thought, this is not going very well.
So he decided to back out of the situation and embark upon a new strategy, which would be more sensibly advised by a military strategist — which was: don’t attack your enemy’s strongest point, deal with some weaker points. So therefore he decided to attack other people than China.
He tried to do a deal with Russia first. That wasn’t an attack on Russia, because the biggest problem for Trump is the relations between Russia and China, and therefore he tried what is known as a reverse Kissinger or reverse Nixon — that is, to try to separate Russia from China. That’s named after Nixon and Kissinger’s famous trip to China in 1972, to attempt, successfully, due to the stupid policies of the Soviet leadership, to detach China from Russia. In this case it was to detach Russia from China.
But that didn’t go very well, because, one, Putin is certainly not an idiot and understands that if the United States succeeded in defeating China, the United States would then turn around and attack Russia. And due to the situation in the United States, they were not prepared to make enough concessions over the question of Ukraine. So that didn’t go well.
So then Trump — apart from another thing, which was to use military attacks, or military-related attacks, on a series of Global South countries which were seen as favourable to China and not in the interest of the United States. He obviously had a big success in Venezuela. Cuba turned out to be a very much tougher nut to crack than he thought, and that situation has become threatening. That situation may escalate — there are discussions at the moment in the United States about invading Cuba. We’ll see whether that develops or not. But despite the oil blockade, Cuba has not shown any signs of giving in.
And of course he launched the war against Iran, which has gone very seriously wrong. Let’s say, okay, this is a fifteen-round contest and we’re probably up to about round five — but so far Iran’s won all five of the rounds, and therefore that’s not going very well. In fact, it’s going badly.
So under those circumstances, launching a frontal attack on China at the present time, he needs like a hole in the head.
So therefore that’s why the situation produced a situation of relative stability. It means two contending forces are pressing against each other; they have approximately equal strength in the present situation, therefore the situation doesn’t shift much. That’s why I think the situation is relatively stable in the short term — because of the strength of China.
That therefore explains why there was a summit with a great deal of pageantry, which is significant

articles.title_orig: Chinese language teachers leave the Philippines over safety fears
articles.title_zh: Chinese language teachers leave the Philippines over safety fears
articles.content_orig:
Educational exchanges are in the firing line as tensions between the two countries spill over into the classroom
Around 150 Chinese language teachers in the Philippines are returning home following mounting criticism from Philippine security officials that educational exchanges involving China could pose national security threats.
The withdrawal affects teachers stationed at schools including the Immaculate Conception Academy in Greenhills and Jubilee Christian Academy in Quezon City, both in Metro Manila, according to local media.
The Manila-based Chinese Commercial News reported on Friday that the inviting organisations – the Philippine Chinese Education Research Centre and the Federation of Filipino-Chinese Chambers of Commerce and Industry – made the decision after families of Chinese instructors expressed safety concerns amid growing scrutiny of Chinese educational programmes.
The report said that Chinese teachers left the Philippines on Thursday.

articles.title_orig: The world’s 10 most stress-free destinations
articles.title_zh: The world’s 10 most stress-free destinations
articles.content_orig:
Emma is a freelance travel journalist and long-standing contributor to The Telegraph. She is the recipient of several writing awards and has twice been named BGTW Travel Writer of the Year. She has spoken as a travel expert at the Royal Geographical Society, the Frontline Club and National Geographic headquarters in Washington DC and her Scottish lilt can occasionally be heard on the BBC’s From Our Own Correspondent. She can be contacted via Instagram at @emmathomsontravels
Emails. Phone calls. Appointments. Passwords. Protein. Water. Eight hours of sleep. Our lives have become a relentless pursuit of doing – and doing everything better. Even travelling can become a to-do list of bucket-list experiences, country counts and “Instagrammable” moments.
The antidote? The (admittedly laughably named) “stillcation” – a new way of holidaying that pushes back against our culture of constant productivity and self-improvement.
It’s not necessarily yoga at sunrise or a silent meditation retreat, although it can be. More simply, it’s about the absence of agenda. Of stripping life back to its essentials: good food, beautiful views, fresh air and anchoring yourself in the present moment. Instead of seeking destinations that offer the most to do, it asks where offers the best conditions for doing less.
“Man’s inability to sit quietly in a room alone” was, according to French philosopher Blaise Pascal, the source of all humanity’s problems. Four centuries later, his observation feels oddly prescient. We are rarely sitting still – even when on holiday.
The constant pressure to optimise our lives can lead to chronic dysregulation of the nervous system, says Jamie Clements, a wellness retreat facilitator and author of the upcoming book The Next Breath . “Stress has become the baseline, and calm feels like the exception.”
Tour operators are catching onto our increasing thirst for deeper ways to unplug. Inghams recently ranked almost 100 European destinations according to their “stillest”, with criteria including walking trails per square kilometre, air quality, birdsong richness, stargazing quality, human density and forest cover (Scotland’s Wester Ross, see below, took the top spot).
Black Tomato is designing itineraries centred around themes such as “The Gift of Boredom” and “Sonic Sanctuaries”, with quiet-hour museum slots and low-stimulation dining. We’ve also seen a proliferation of Unplugged detox cabins and AirBnbs offering Wi-Fi and technology-free countryside boltholes.
Slowing down switches our nervous system from a fight-or-flight sympathetic state to a rest-and-digest parasympathetic system that lowers blood pressure and improves concentration by possibly stimulating neurogenesis – the creation of new brain cells.
But don’t assume that a stillcation will immediately evoke a state of inward zen. Like any other holiday – where it can take a week to unwind – the first day or two can feel uncomfortable.
The point of a stillcation isn’t simply that sitting around feels nice. Removing the constant demand for attention – and replacing the thrum of traffic, screens and notifications with wind, water, birdsong and walking – may create the conditions in which both mind and body can begin to really recover.
And the benefits extend beyond our own wellbeing. Several of the qualities that make a destination “still” – low population density, dark skies, forests, clean air, biodiversity and quiet trails – are also qualities that depend on healthy, protected environments.
Perhaps that is the real appeal of the stillcation. It doesn’t ask us to abandon movement, curiosity or adventure. It simply changes the objective. Travel becomes less about collecting experiences and more about noticing where we are; less about escaping life and more about inhabiting it. In a culture that has turned even rest into something to optimise, doing nothing might be the most radical itinerary of all.
Lungfuls of salty Cornish coastal air, strolls along the South West Coast Path and its secluded beaches, plus one of the UK’s last remaining temperate rainforests make this the ideal space to slow down.
How to do it: Jamie Clements offers a four-day breathwork retreat at Cabilla in Cornwall from £1,250 per person.
Wester Ross – in the remote north-west highlands of Scotland – is an unspoilt mash of moorlands and mountains that is home to pine martens, otters and the elusive wild cat. Its minimal light pollution creates star-rich dark skies.
How to do it: Wildlife Worldwide offer a six-day The Splendours of Wester Ross tour from £1,295 per person.
Glimpse magic in this Swedish Lapland village that’s probably one of the best places on Earth to see the northern lights (September–April) due to its cloud-free “blue hole”.
How to do it: Arctic Direct offer a three-night Abisko tour from £1,795 per person, including flights and activities.
Creating a wrinkled border between France and Spain, the bird-rich Pyrenees are scarce on people and big on open spaces for mindful hiking, yoga and thermal spas to unwind.
How to do it: Much Better Adventures offer a six-night Hike and Wild Swim in the French Pyrenees tour from £1,688 per person, excluding flights.
Switzerland’s “secret valley” is scattered with lö da ler (wooden cabins with books and reading benches), mindful running trails and forest bathing opportunities, including the Senda Botanica – a narrow path through 30 species of trees.
How to do it: Inntravel offer a seven-night Walking and Wildflowers in the Engadine Valley guided tour from £2,086 per person, excluding flights.
Described as one of the last pristine wilderness areas left on Earth, Yukon has a population of about 48,000 people spread across a territory roughly the size of Spain. It offers an extraordinary sense of space for hiking, wildlife watching, paddling and simply being outdoors.
How to do it: Canadian Sky offer a 10-night In the Footsteps of the Yukon Pioneers self-drive tour from £2,069 per person, including flights.
New Zealand ranks second in the world for peacefulness, behind Iceland. Pick the South Island’s Fiordland, Glenorchy and wild West Coast for vast mountains, sparse settlements and trails where the only itinerary is to walk, breathe and look.
How to do it: Pure Pods has off-grid glass cabins scattered across New Zealand from £240 per night.
Mountain trails, monasteries lit by butter lamps and a deliberately low-volume tourism model make Bhutan in south Asia particularly well suited to a holiday centred on contemplation rather than consumption.
How to do it: Raven Tours offer a nine-day Yoga, Culture and Stillness in the Kingdom of Happiness tour from £2,676 per person based on two sharing.
Nowhere serves up remote stillness quite like Torres del Paine National Park. A raw jostle of glacial lakes, mountains and clear air, it is ideal for forest bathing and restorative walking.
How to do it: Chile Nativo offer a five-day Torres del Paine Wellness Retreat from £1,700 per person from October to April, excluding flights.
One of the world’s least densely populated countries, Namibia in southern Africa is home to the oldest desert in the world, exceptionally dark skies and remarkable wildlife. Don’t miss Sossusvlei, Damaraland and the stark Skeleton Coast.
How to do it: Expert Africa offer a 14-day Discover Namibia self-drive safari from £4,220 per person based on two sharing.

articles.title_orig: Failed ‘torturous’ execution attempt on Christa Pike reignites death penalty debate
articles.title_zh: Failed ‘torturous’ execution attempt on Christa Pike reignites death penalty debate
articles.content_orig:
Media witnesses recount the moments before the execution of Christa Pike was halted Wednesday in Nashville, Tenn. George Walker IV/AP hide caption
The botched execution in Tennessee of Christa Pike, who survived despite being subject to two doses of lethal injection on Wednesday, has reignited furious debate about the death penalty in the U.S.
Witnesses say Pike, who was strapped to a gurney, was administered a supposedly lethal dose of the barbiturate pentobarbital but after several minutes said her arm was burning and asked if it was supposed to feel that way. She then asked "please try up on my shoulder higher."
A second dose was administered, and the 50-year-old, who has been on death row for murder since she was 18, appeared to fall unconscious but continued breathing and snoring. Her lawyers made emergency calls, and the execution was halted. Pike was taken to the hospital, where she remains in critical condition and is being given "lifesaving care," according to her lawyers. It is unclear yet whether she has suffered brain damage.
"We at this point do not know the ramifications of the chemical torture that she has endured," Pike's attorney Randy Spivey said in a video press briefing , calling what happened in the death chamber "torturous" and "cruel."
The Death Penalty Information Center (DPI), a nonpartisan nonprofit organization, said Pike was the first person in the history of capital punishment to survive after being injected with lethal drugs. Other people have survived failed attempts to execute them when execution staff were unable to establish IV lines.
"This failed attempt is the worst we've ever seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era," said Robin M. Maher, DPI executive director, in a statement.
"What happened to Christa Pike can be attributed to the extreme secrecy Tennessee officials have maintained about their execution procedures, their refusal to answer reasonable questions, and their unwillingness to accept responsibility for their mistakes," she continued. The media are not allowed to witness key portions of the process, including the insertion of IV lines.
Pike, who was convicted of and admitted to the 1995 murder of fellow teenager and classmate Colleen Slemmer, who she saw as a love rival, would have been the first woman to be executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. But it was the second botched attempt in the state this year, after Tennessee stopped the execution of Tony Carruthers in May when medical workers were unable to insert a second IV line.
Gov. Bill Lee, a Republican, has now called off executions in the state for the rest of the year. He has launched an investigation into what happened to Pike and said the botched execution "shouldn't have happened." However, he stressed at a press conference that "the people of Tennessee have determined that the death penalty is the appropriate penalty for the most heinous crimes in the state."
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who is running to replace Lee, agreed, but said the state should "bring back the electric chair" rather than using lethal injection.
However, Blackburn's Democratic opponent, Jerri Green, condemned the practice, saying: "The fact of the matter is: the death penalty has always been inhumane, expensive, and biased."
"As a public defender, I've met a few too many people who were wrongfully convicted on death row who were later exonerated … If we say we are pro-life, that means we must be anti-death penalty," her statement read.
Kathleen Walter prays in the area reserved for people opposed to the death penalty outside Riverbend Maximum Security Institution before the planned execution of Christa Pike on Wednesday in Nashville, Tenn. George Walker IV/AP hide caption
In May, fellow Democrats Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., and Rep. Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass., reintroduced legislation to try to abolish the death penalty, after the Department of Justice announced it was bringing back firing squads. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
"The death penalty is not a punishment reserved for the worst of the worst; it is one reserved for the poorest of the poor. And it is a penalty disproportionately faced by Black Americans," said Durbin at the time.
"It is far from clear that the death penalty even serves its primary purpose. There has yet to be any evidence conclusively demonstrating that the death penalty deters people from committing heinous crimes compared to the threat of life in prison," he said.
Americans' opinions on capital punishment have shifted over the decades, a Gallup Poll shows. The 1960s were the last time approval for the death penalty dropped below 50%. Approval was at its highest in the mid-1990s, but has dropped again since, with 52% of respondents saying they favored the death penalty in 2025.
On Thursday, International rights watchdog Amnesty International called on the U.S. to abolish the death penalty, saying : "As the death penalty continues to decline around the world, the United States remains increasingly isolated."
Executions in the U.S. have been on the rise. Last year, 47 people were put to death nationwide, the most since 2009. Data shows Florida carried out the most executions, accounting for 19 of those carried out last year.
Methods also differ across states, with the majority of executions in 2025 carried out by lethal injection. However, three were by firing squad and five were by nitrogen inhalation, which United Nations experts have said is akin to "state-sanctioned torture."

articles.title_orig: US and China release $60 billion nonsensitive product lists for tariff cuts after Trump-Xi meeting
articles.title_zh: US and China release $60 billion nonsensitive product lists for tariff cuts after Trump-Xi meeting
articles.content_orig:
HONG KONG (AP) — The United States and China on Monday released reciprocal lists of nonsensitive products worth about $30 billion each that will see tariff cuts, from American hair products to Chinese toys, in a deal expected to help bolster bilateral trade.
The details came days after Chinese President Xi Jinping met with U.S. President Donald Trump in Washington in his first state visit to the U.S. since 2015. The U.S. had already reduced tariffs against China after Trump’s tariffs reached as high as 145% at one point last year, as tensions between the two countries eased.

articles.title_orig: Uzbekistan dominates chess Olympiad while England’s Sivanandan, 11, sets new world age record
articles.title_zh: Uzbekistan dominates chess Olympiad while England’s Sivanandan, 11, sets new world age record
articles.content_orig:
Host nation won having led almost from start to finish, while young English player reached a stunning landmark
Uzbekistan, the host nation, won the open gold medals at the 2026 Olympiad, the biennial chess international team tournament, at Samarkand last week in the style of the legendary Soviet grandmasters of long ago. India, the defending champions, were second, Germany a surprise third, and the top-seeded United States fourth.
The hosts led almost from start to finish, with world No 5 Nodirbek Abdusattorov and the world title challenger Javokhir Sindarov their top-board powerhouses. The team recovered swiftly from a single defeat by Germany, and were particularly impressive in crushing Armenia by 3.5-0.5 in the penultimate round. The Uzbekistan government rewarded each of the five players with $200,000 (£178,000), a house and a Volkswagen, plus $50,000 for the coach Rustam Kasimdzhanov.
India performed in line with their seeding. Putting the world champion, Gukesh Dommaraju, on board four boosted his results but also underlined that Sindarov is the favourite for the coming world championship match. Gukesh was exposed in the final rounds when he was outplayed against both Germany, although he won that game fortuitously, and Hungary.
The final leading scores were: Uzbekistan 20/22 match points; India and Germany 18 ; USA, Azerbaijan, Armenia and Hungary 17 ; China, France, Spain, Ukraine and England 16 (206 teams competed).
England’s creditable 12th place, one below their seeding, would have been still higher if a third player had performed at the level of the nine-time British champion Michael Adams, 54, and the Spectator chess columnist Luke McShane, 42, who were both in contention for individual medals right up to the final round. England’s women were 15th against their seeding of 20th, and the combined performance was the best since at least 2018, and probably since 1990.
Russia/USSR, which monopolised Olympiad golds in the second half of the 20th century, have been banned from the last three competitions due to the invasion of Ukraine. If allowed to take part, a team of Ian Nepomniachtchi, Andrey Esipenko, Daniil Dubov, Vladislav Artemiev and Alexander Grischuk would have been contenders.
The potential of Turkey’s Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus stands out. The 15-year-old won the individual silver medal unbeaten and has advanced to No 17 in the live ratings, a similar level to Bobby Fischer at that age and well ahead of current world No 1 Carlsen when he was 15. Here he defeats a rival prodigy , Argentina’s Faustino Oro.
China won the women’s Olympiad ahead of Kazakhstan, India and the US, and did so with its B team. World champion Ju Wenjun, world No 1 Hou Yifan, former title challenger Tan Zhongyi and world No 3 Lei Tingjie all stayed at home, but their substitutes, led by world No 4 Zhu Jiner and 16-year-old Lu Miaoyi, proved highly effective.
For the future, the US is potentially a powerhouse in women’s chess. Its duo of Carissa Yip, 23, and Alice Lee, 16, are both targeting the open GM title and its $100,000 bonus offered by Dr Jeanne Cairns Sinquefield, while new candidates are emerging in Rachael Li, Rose Atwell and Zoey Tang who are all teenagers with 2300+ ratings.
Bodhana Sivanandan broke the world age record for the youngest ever woman grandmaster (WGM). Her 8/11 total, playing all games with no rest days, included six wins, draws against Ukraine’s reigning European champion Anastasiia Hnatyshyn and Georgia’s former World Blitz champion Nana Dzagnidze, both of them current world top 20 players, and a solitary loss to Deysi Cori of Peru due to a time-pressure blunder in a drawn ending.
The 11-year-old Harrow schoolgirl’s record as the youngest ever WGM broke Hou’s 2006 mark by several months, and she also recorded her second norm (of three needed) for the international master (IM) title at open level. For IM, she also needs a 2400 rating against her current 2382, which includes the Olympiad.
Her last-round Olympiad game was a model of what has become her trademark style of a Magnus Carlsen grind.
If she secures her final norm and becomes an IM before her 12th birthday, she will break the all-time female No 1 Judit Polgar’s world age record and also become one of the 10 youngest ever IMs. She is already No 2 among all players born in 2015, behind only Russia’s IM Roman Shogdzhiev, who has been groomed for several years as a potential heir to Anatoly Karpov.
after newsletter promotion
The Guardian’s Matthew Weaver interviewed Sivanandan after her return home. At the end of the Olympiad the youngster talked with Lichess.org’s Theo Wait , while chess.com also covered her achievements in detail .
The Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport’s new £250,000 a year Supporting Elite Chess Fund document contains no specific provision for rewarding world-record breakers. Maybe it should, as Sivanandan’s IM title and new record could follow as soon as the London Classic, which begins in November.
Sivanandan has just started at secondary school, and that could slow her progress on the chessboard. The advance from IM to GM is difficult, and many talents eventually plateau, which should temper extrapolations of a rise comparable to Polgar and Hou.
Meanwhile Timur Turlov, 38, a Russian-born entrepreneur from Kazakhstan whose company Freedom Holding has a multibillion dollar valuation on the Nasdaq index, was elected as the new president of the world chess body Fide last Saturday.
The previous Fide President, Russia’s Arkady Dvorkovich, had planned to run for a third term but was forced to withdraw due to EU sanctions on his assets and travel visas.
Turlov received 96 votes against 76 for the German businessman Wadim Rosenstein and a surprisingly low 20 for the ticket of Jan Henric Buettner of Freestyle Chess and the ECF’s international director Malcolm Pein. In the run-off ballot they switched to Turlov, who defeated Rosenstein 110-85.
Turlov is young, committed and with proven business skills. However, there could be an immediate problem since Rosenstein has appealed to the court of arbitration for sport over the new president’s eligibility.

articles.title_orig: Nike shares plummet 10% after weak revenue outlook and layoff plans underway
articles.title_zh: Nike shares plummet 10% after weak revenue outlook and layoff plans underway
articles.content_orig:
Nike's shares plummeted in premarket trading Friday, falling for a second straight day after it reported falling revenue and plans to lay off staff in 2027.
The sportswear giant said Thursday that its fiscal first-quarter revenues were down 4% to $11.2 billion, citing declines in Greater China, which was partially offset by growth in its North America segment. Its net income was  $712 million, down 2% from $727 million the previous year.
"We have more work to do in NIKE Sportswear, Jordan Brand and Greater China, and we're taking deliberate actions to strengthen those businesses the right way for the long term," Nike President and CEO Elliott Hill said in the release.
Nike expects revenues to decline in the high-single digits in 2027. Its shares were last down 10.36% in premarket trading on Friday and have declined nearly 45% since the beginning of the year.
The company also announced its new operating model "Pace," which is expected to deliver $2.5 billion in cost savings by 2031, with plans to lay off more staff starting in 2027.
"This work will result in fewer roles across Nike, and I want to acknowledge that news like this creates uncertainty. I don't take that lightly," Hill said in a separate announcement on Thursday. "Decisions about impacted roles related to this work will begin in calendar year 2027 and beyond."
The program also includes efforts to modernize Nike's global supply chain, organizing into three geographies, establishing a new campus in India, and further streamlining the organization to reduce costs.
Nike has already carried out layoffs twice since the beginning of the year, including cutting 775 jobs across its U.S. distribution centers in January, and letting go of a further 1,400 employees primarily in its tech division in April.
Citi analysts said in a note Friday that they will remain "neutral" on the company as its sales guidance came in below market expectations.
"Nike is turning into a cost-cutting story, announcing a $2.5bn cost savings program as management is adapting to the reality of significant pressure within Sportswear, Jordan, and China," the Citi analysts said.
They noted that management will offer more detail on its five-year outlook at their investor day, but details around when Pace will actually "move the dial" will only come in 2029.
"It isn't out of the question that Nike can beat some of the guidance they just provided, but there really is no justification (in our view) for Nike to receive a premium multiple versus its growing peers," they added.

articles.title_zh: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq futures rise ahead of key jobs report as oil steadies
articles.content_orig:
Oil prices were sharply lower on Friday morning, extending losses from earlier in the session, following reports of a potential move to release diesel and crude stocks to ease a global supply shortage.
International benchmark Brent crude futures with December expiry traded 3.1% lower at $99.13 per barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures with November expiry fell 4% to $89.18.
It comes shortly after Reuters reported that European Union member states were discussing a French proposal to release additional diesel reserves following pressure from the Trump administration .
The report, which cited a single unnamed source familiar with details of the discussion, said France had proposed that EU nations release 50 million barrels of diesel and International Energy Agency members release 50 million barrels of crude oil.
CNBC could not independently verify the report. A spokesperson for the French government and the IEA were not immediately available to comment.
The EU is holding crisis talks on Friday to discuss a coordinated response to soaring diesel prices after U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called on European countries to urgently release some of the continent's reserves.
In a post on social media, Bessent said Thursday that aAmerica's European partners "should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions."
He added: "American farmers, truckers, and businesses should not be left carrying the burden of a global diesel shortage."
U.S. President Donald Trump , who has repeatedly touted the prospect of a diesel export ban, appeared to cool on the idea earlier this week, following a resurgence in crude exports through the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz.
The U.S. supplied around half of the EU's diesel imports in August, according to the International Energy Agency, underscoring the 27-nation bloc's exposure to a potential export ban.
Oil prices settled higher in the previous session amid a report that the U.S. is sending a third aircraft carrier strike group to the Middle East, along with an amphibious force carrying 2,000 Marines, raising the stakes for an escalation in the months-long conflict.

articles.title_orig: Some of world’s strict aviation security measures are under fresh scrutiny after in-flight attack
articles.title_zh: Some of world’s strict aviation security measures are under fresh scrutiny after in-flight attack
articles.content_orig:
Morning Rundown: How Cornell student reacted to rape accusation, why fewer young people are getting shingles, and poison centers see uptick in ‘cat’s claw’ calls
JERUSALEM — Israel has some of the world’s most stringent air travel security measures. The United Arab Emirates proudly adheres to international aviation safety standards. Yet those safeguards failed to prevent a flight between the countries from taking a dangerous plunge during an alleged attack in the cockpit .
The copilot allegedly stabbed the captain in the cockpit before passengers intervened aboard FlyDubai Flight FZ1073 after taking off from Dubai, UAE, with 182 people including eight crew members flying to Tel Aviv, Israel, on Wednesday.
The airplane made a safe emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday and the incident is under investigation by Saudi, Emirati and Israeli authorities, with the United States and Oman assisting efforts to determine a motive.
“Until this event, the possibility of a threat originating from a pilot or crew member was not considered a likely scenario. Security efforts have traditionally focused much more heavily on passengers and their luggage,” said Eyal Hulata, Israel’s former national security adviser. “That will probably change now and crew members will be subject to heavier screening.”
Israel’s security protocols focus heavily on Israeli airlines and departing flights from Ben-Gurion International Airport. A potential Achilles’ heel lies overseas, where procedures for Israel-bound flights vary and are harder for Israeli authorities to oversee.
Dubai International Airport, the world’s busiest airport for international passenger traffic, has built some of its appeal around a reputation for safety in a volatile region, said Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in England.
“They are very conscious of the fact, a little bit like Israel in many respects, that they cannot afford to have a terrorist attack happening on a flight out of there,” he said.
Pilot vetting and preflight screening aren’t uniform worldwide.
Investigators have not publicly identified the object used to stab the flight’s captain or said whether it was carried onto the plane or came from inside the aircraft.
Preflight screening of flight crews should generally “mirror very closely what a passenger goes through,” although security procedures vary around the world, said Dave Komendat, a senior security adviser at risk management firm International SOS and former chief security officer for Boeing.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Thursday that Israel has long-standing agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots from flying into the country if they are citizens of nations that don’t maintain diplomatic relations with Israel.
Israeli authorities have described the FlyDubai copilot as Omani. Israel and Oman do not have formal diplomatic relations, raising questions about how the suspect ended up on the Tel Aviv-bound flight.
“Obviously, there was a loophole here. And we’re taking care of that,” Netanyahu said Thursday during an interview with Fox News Channel’s “Fox and Friends.”
Israel will increase security precautions on flights coming into the country whether or not they are operated by Israel. Pilots flying into Israel will be vetted and Israel will know their identities, prime minister’s office spokesperson Doron Spielman told The Associated Press.
There were no Israeli air marshals on the FlyDubai flight and the people who helped were civilians, Spielman added.
The International Civil Aviation Organization sets baseline pilot-vetting and licensing standards, while national regulators and airlines can impose additional requirements.
Aviation security expert Menachem Bachrach said Israel relies largely on foreign governments and airlines to vet their own crew members, and Wednesday’s incident may point to a compliance lapse rather than a flaw in the procedures.
“Before we’re jumping to tighten security, I would just say it’s likely that somebody didn’t follow the protocols,” Bachrach said.
Investigators to look for red flags and review distress call handling
Israeli flag carrier El Al periodically assesses its pilots’ fitness to fly, while other airlines may do so less often, said Arik Arad, chairman of the aviation cybersecurity consultancy CYVIATION and El Al’s former head of security at Ben Gurion Airport.
Investigators will want to know whether colleagues previously reported concerns about the copilot and, if so, how the airline responded, Komendat said.
Investigators in the UAE and Israel also are likely to review responses to the distress signals that came from the FlyDubai plane after a steep drop in altitude.
A person who heard the FlyDubai flight’s air traffic control communications said a crew member reported a hijacking and requested ambulances. Authorities in Saudi Arabia and Jordan initially refused to clear the aircraft for landing, said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
The crew member eventually persuaded Saudi authorities to allow the plane to set down at Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport in the city of Tabuk.
International aviation standards call for countries to give aircraft facing hijacking or other “unlawful interference” maximum assistance and priority. But the underlying 1944 treaty, the Convention on International Civil Aviation, only requires a country to provide assistance “as it may find practicable,” making it a “relatively soft obligation,” said Vincent Correia, co-director of McGill University’s Institute of Air and Space Law.
Standard practice in a serious emergency is to get an aircraft on the ground as quickly as possible at the nearest suitable runway, “regardless of nationality, flight plan or politics,” said John Gradek, who manages McGill’s Aviation Management Program.
Gradek stressed it’s still not clear why the FlyDubai plane took a 180-degree turn as it crossed into Jordanian airspace before heading southwest to Tabuk. It’s not unusual for flight crews to bypass the nearest airport in favor of one better-equipped to meet a plane’s needs, he said.
Locked cockpits have been central to flight security for 25 years
Netanyahu said the flight’s injured captain saved the aircraft and the 182 people on it by resisting the copilot’s attacks long enough to open the 737’s cockpit door, enabling passengers to subdue the suspect and other FlyDubai crew members to take the controls and land the plane.
Cockpit doors worldwide were reinforced and locked after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks to keep intruders out. The FlyDubai incident, and past crashes caused by pilots who wanted to take their own lives, highlight the risk when a threat comes from inside the cockpit.
“The industry itself needs to recognize that flight deck door — whilst installed for very understandable reasons to prevent a suicidal hijacking by a passenger — has also created a fortress into which the good guys cannot gain access to a rogue individual, be it a hijacker or a rogue crew member,” Baum said.
Airline personnel know more about aviation security weaknesses and can gain the trust of security workers they regularly encounter, Osprey Flight Solutions Chief Intelligence Officer Matthew Borie, whose company advises airlines on flight threats, said.
“Unfortunately, if an insider with nefarious intent wants to carry out something like this, they may actually be best placed to know where the most vulnerable points are and how to breach them,” Borie said.

articles.title_orig: Removing Red Tape Won’t Erase China’s Mining Advantage in Africa
articles.title_zh: Removing Red Tape Won’t Erase China’s Mining Advantage in Africa
articles.content_orig:
Recently, the top executive of KoBold Metals, a U.S. mineral exploration and development company, told Reuters that Western companies could catch up and compete effectively with Chinese companies in Africa if only red tape were removed .
I have to say, I was surprised by his confidence. Red tape is often blamed for the complexity and the lack of transparency of mining licensing and operations in Africa. Combined with the risks associated with many African mining jurisdictions, it can certainly deter Western capital.
Western companies would probably, as some might believe, be more competitive without the bureaucratic hurdles that slow them down. Chinese companies would welcome the removal of some of those hurdles too, even if they are less likely to say so publicly.
It’s not that Chinese companies are happy to deal with red tape, as some seem to believe. Speak with Chinese mining operators in Africa and you quickly understand how much they hate red tape; they deal with the same delays, uncertainty, and bureaucracy that frustrate their Western counterparts.
The difference is that many Chinese firms have nevertheless found ways to operate within these environments. How they do that is another question, and it’s not always one with comfortable answers. The lesson is not that Chinese companies have cracked some admirable code for dealing with red tape, but that they have managed to keep operating despite it.
Removing red tape would certainly help. It would reduce risk and bring more predictability to mining jurisdictions, which Chinese and Western companies alike would welcome. But I’m not so sure that alone would allow Western companies to catch up, as KoBold president Josh Goldman suggests.
Can Western companies match Chinese companies in their ability to raise and deploy capital, especially when Chinese companies can draw on state financing and other forms of government support? Can Western companies come with the whole package, offering infrastructure, financing, and commercial investment? Can Western companies match the political capital that Chinese companies have built over years in these countries — relationships that have helped some companies survive changes of administration and regime while maintaining their operations?
I have my opinions on how that competition would play out. We might even get a chance to see it in action, in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where authorities are considering a one-stop shop to process billion-dollar mining projects regardless of investors’ origin. Politics and geopolitics aside, I’d be curious to see how Western companies would fare against their Chinese competitors under those conditions.
Then we might find out how much of the gap is really about red tape.
C. Geraud Neema is CGSP’s Africa Editor.

articles.title_orig: Lutheran identity in Norway and the United Kingdom
articles.title_zh: Lutheran identity in Norway and the United Kingdom
articles.content_orig:
Reflections on mission, identity and ecumenical relations were high on the agenda during a visit to London and Oxford by leaders of one of Norway’s northernmost dioceses.
Bishop Svein Valle (fourth from right) with deans from the diocese of Sør-Hålogaland in front of St Olav’s Norwegian church in London. Photo: LWF/P. Hitchen
(LWI) - A recent visit to St Olav’s Norwegian church in London felt a bit like a homecoming for Bishop Svein Valle, who leads the diocese of Sør-Hålogaland in northern Norway. Almost 30 years ago, he came to London with his wife and two young children to serve as chaplain to the congregation, which is also known as the Norwegian Church Abroad, or the Norwegian Seamen’s Mission.
“We were a bit adventurous and we wanted to experience something new,” he recalls, sitting in the sanctuary of the church, where the Norwegian government-in-exile regularly worshipped during the Second World War. Norway’s recently deceased King Harald was also a regular visitor and the church became a focal point for hundreds of his countrymen and women who gathered to attend memorial events following his death in August.
In the late 1990s, when Valle came to London (he began his ministry on the day that Princess Diana died), he says that many of his duties were still strongly connected with the support of maritime workers docking on the banks of the River Thames. “Norwegian ships were coming in all along the Thames, with sugar cane, or carbon dioxide to put in the beer, or oil tankers coming in from the North Sea. We visited all of them. We knew where the crews were from and we brought them newspapers from different regions of Norway,” he says.
How are we going to remain a church in 50 or 100 years?
Bishop Svein Valle, Church of Norway Diocese of Sør-Hålogaland
Three decades on, the bishop was back in Britain leading a delegation of deans from his diocese for a visit to London and Oxford, where they attended both traditional and contemporary worship services and held discussions on mission with their Anglican counterparts. “Our goal was to see what others are doing in the Church of England, where they have an ambitious plan to double the numbers of youth and children attending church by 2030,” he says, noting that declining membership is a challenge facing both Lutheran and Anglican churches.
The Church of Norway is a member of the Porvoo Communion of Lutheran and Anglican churches in Europe that have established full communion between and among themselves.
While the Church of Norway membership numbers around 60 percent of the population nationwide and 70 percent in his own diocese, Valle says he sees the trends elsewhere in Europe as “a warning sign.” Together with his deans, he has been reflecting on “how are we going to remain a church in 50 or 100 years? We know we need to do something today, so it was interesting to share ideas and to hear some Anglican perspectives.”
During his time as chaplain at St Olav’s church, he enjoyed close relations with Anglican and Catholic priests in his part of the city, located alongside one of the first tunnels for transport underneath the Thames. “We had monthly meetings with colleagues from the two Anglican churches, one a very low [charismatic] church and one a high [traditional] church, as well as with the priests from two Catholic parishes,” he remembers.
Bishop Svein Valle (right) with LWF Council member Dean Kristine Sandmæl in the sanctuary of St Olav’s Norwegian church in London. Photo: LWF/P. Hitchen
The visiting Church of Norway delegation deep in discussions inside St Olav’s Norwegian church in London. Photo: LWF/P. Hitchen
St Olav’s Norwegian church in London. Photo: LWF/P. Hitchen
“I feel that today we need to think more about so-called ‘mixed ecology’ church, which has different shapes and different people can find things to relate to,” he continues, reflecting on the outcome of 19 to 22 September visit. “What we do in Norway is fairly traditional, although we have choirs and youth clubs and some activities for toddlers too. But we can see that when children are attracted and regularly attend, they are socialized into the church and into the faith,” he says.
“There is a greater diversity within the Church of England, from very evangelical ways of worshipping to very traditional liturgy and music,” notes Dean Kristine Sandmæl , a member of The Lutheran World Federation (LWF) Council and a participant in the diocesan visit to Britain. “We know that our youth work needs refreshment, but how you do church in a big city with a university will always be very different from doing church in a small village with mostly older people,” she says. “The evangelical model is popular with young people, but it also comes with a more conservative theology and ethical perspectives and this is a big challenge,” she reflects.
Unlike the Anglican church in Britain, Lutherans in this country have always been a small minority, notes Sandmæl at the conclusion of the first in-person meeting of the bishop and all the deans in the diocese. “We have three new members of our team, so this has been an important time for all of us to reflect together,” she says. “Where we come from, people are just members of the majority church and don’t think so much about what it means to be Lutheran. I think this visit has challenged us to think more deeply about strengthening our Lutheran identity in our own context,” she concludes.

In East Africa , prolonged rainfall deficits since around April and high temperatures resulted in below average yields in many areas, including main producing regions in Ethiopia and western Kenya.

In the Middle East & North Africa , rice prospects remain favourable in Egypt, Iraq, and Iran, and land preparation is beginning for the upcoming 2026/27 wheat season.
In Southern Africa , winter wheat prospects have degraded in the main producing region of South Africa due to recent dry impacts. Elsewhere, in Zimbabwe and Zambia wheat prospects remain favourable.
In Central & South Asia , the 2025/26 spring wheat harvest is underway with generally favourable conditions with some areas of dryness.
In Southeast Asia , conditions are generally favourable for dry-season rice and maize in the south, while drought is negatively impacting wet-season crops in Thailand and Cambodia, and heavy rains are negatively impacting parts of the Philippines, Vietnam and Myanmar.
In Central America & the Caribbean , harvesting of Primera season crops is complete, and below average yields resulted across the region due to prolonged dry spells and high temperatures since the start of the season.

articles.title_orig: Powering China, reshaping Tibet
articles.title_zh: Powering China, reshaping Tibet
articles.content_orig:
To play this audio please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Send a voice message to LivingPlanet
Subscribe to the podcast here via your favorite podcast app: Living Planet Podlink
Lobsang Yangtso: We would just lie down and then, you know, drink directly from the river with your mouth, and then I have this memory because when I turned over that side, you know, I could see a horse drinking at the same time as well. [laughs] Yeah, I mean, I remember that part. Yeah, I mean, you can just you know lie down … and drink directly from the river. You are making me to miss my homeland. [laughs]
For the first twenty years of her life, Lobsang Yangtso lives in eastern Tibet. Then she leaves. Twenty-five years pass before she comes home again.
Lobsang Yangtso: But now, you know, everything has changed.
The Tibet she returns is not the Tibet she remembers.
The no mads gone from the hills where she’d watched them grazing. Instead fences cut across the landscape. CCTV towers overlook villages. And the river from her childhood?
Nobody drinks there anymore, Lobsang says.
But what she's seeing in her hometown is part of something much bigger.
Around the world, countries are racing to cut carbon emissions - and demand is soaring for the resources needed to build a cleaner energy system.
No country is moving faster than China. It leads the world in building solar panels, wind farms, batteries and electric vehicles.
And much of what China needs is found on the Tibetan Plateau: rivers that feed some of Asia’s largest watersheds, along with copper, lithium and other critical minerals.
But this isn’t just a story about energy. It’s about land, culture and power - and who pays the price for progress.
Lobsang Yangtso: my homeland is one of the most beautiful places in Tibet. …
Today Lobsang Yangtso is an environmental researcher for International Tibet Network. As a kid, she ran through fields here, in high-altitude farmland surrounded by mountains. River gorges wind through the region. In the nineties, the mountainsides were dotted with slow-moving yaks, and semi-nomadic herders like Lobsang’s father.
Lobsang Yangtso: "...a few families would take all the yaks from all the households and then they go up on the mountain and then they come back. So it's based on the rotation, and they move from place to place. So it's like a very close way, supporting each other, living together and then especially during summer times, because of the high altitude, we get lots of you know the summer flowers...
Yellow poppies. Purple aster. White wild flowers that she can’t recall the name for.
Lobsang Yangtso: "...and people love to go for picnics, and it becomes community picnics. They love to keep horses in their houses as well. Tibet has lots of glaciers and streams and the small rivers are quite you know common."
In the summer, the river was still cool, fed by snowmelt from soaring mountain peaks. And in the winter, when it froze over...
Lobsang Yangtso: "...then ice skating was quite popular, even though we don't have a you know ice proper ice skating that we see, but … you would see small kids. You know, they have a small wooden chair or something like that, and then your friends pushing you, and then you’re just rowing. We have this belief of believing in the sacred mountain and sacred rivers, and because we believe in deities … we believe that if we exploit or extract any of the resources, or create pollution in that area, because of the deities, you know there is a possibility that you get harmed by that."
Lobsang left Tibet as a teenager. A monk from her village gave his blessing, and she was off to India for university. She didn’t know then that coming home would be so hard.
In the years that followed, the Chinese state imposed more and more restrictions on Tibet.
It took twenty-five years for Lobsang to get a visa to go home. Once she did, she wanted to lay eyes on the monastery she grew up worshipping in.
In the monastery, monks wore the same red robes. Police wore plain clothes.
Lobsang: "Even within the monastery, I could see a police station in the monastery."
Law enforcement had entered the monastery. What had vanished were images of the Dalai Lama, the Buddhist spiritual leader who fled to India in the 1950s, only a few years after Tibet was formally incorporated into the People’s Republic of China.
It was not only the monasteries that had changed. So had the land.
Lobsang: "When I was coming inside from Tendu to my hometown, another really strange thing that I have seen is that the sand mining that they do along the rivers."
Tibetan herders were reporting fish disappearing, and hundreds of yaks dying after drinking polluted water.  Locals said the pollution was a brew of toxic chemicals, leaking from mines upstream. The state is digging for what some call the white gold of the green transition – lithium.
Lobsang: "The river that used to flow in just in front of my house, people don't drink anymore."
Many of Asia’s largest rivers originate in the Tibetan Plateau – that’s why this region is called the "Water Tower of Asia." Downstream, an estimated two billion people rely on the flows that begin in this region.
But it’s not just freshwater that matters here. Today, the Tibetan Plateau is dotted with some of the highest saltwater lakes on Earth. And some of those lakes are reservoirs of liquid treasure: lithium, which we need for the batteries that are so crucial to the clean energy transition.
Meanwhile, locked into the rock of these mountains…
Copper and other materials mined here go into the solar panels that China produces so efficiently.
Some of the largest mines under Chinese state control are in Tibet, pumping out hundreds of thousands of tonnes of copper and other minerals each year.
But the mountains hold another prize for the clean energy transition … gravity.
Ruth Gamble: "The place with the most hydropower potential in Asia– well, actually the world, is the water falling off the sides of the east and the south of the Tibetan Plateau, so that's where the dams have been concentrated in the last-- since the since the end of the Three Gorges Dam in the last 25 years.
My name's Ruth Gamble. I'm the director of La Trobe Asia and a senior lecturer in environmental history at La Trobe University in Melbourne, Australia."
Dams work by storing water… and then letting it drop. The force of that fall turns turbines, and their spinning generates electricity.
Ruth Gamble: "What you have like on the edges of the Tibetan plateau where the water just pachooos down That's a technical term – pachooing [laughs] is where it just charges down off the side of the plateau – it’s the most potential energy, gross potential energy of any water on the planet because the descent is so steep, and the descent is so long, that it can it can create more turning turbines. It will turn more turbines than anywhere else on Earth."
All that falling water makes Tibet one of the most promising places on Earth for hydropower. But…
Ruth Gamble: "Everything else wants to slide down there as well. So landslides and avalanches and outburst floods are all going to come charging down that side of the slope as well."
The advocacy group International Campaign for Tibet counts more than 100 dams planned for Tibet that haven’t broken ground yet. They estimate these projects could displace more than a million people. But, they also estimate these dams would produce enough clean energy to electrify a country with the power footprint of Germany – so projects that could push a million people out of their homes could power tens of millions more with renewable energy.
Ruth Gamble: "It’s not just about whether you transition; it's about how you transition, right?"
China is still the world’s largest carbon emitter, and it’s still building coal plants at a cracking pace. Yet its clean energy buildout is also the fastest in the world, by a wide margin. To wrap our heads aro

articles.title_orig: Patient dies by suicide after "insurance issue" delayed medicine for lung disease flare-ups
articles.title_zh: Patient dies by suicide after "insurance issue" delayed medicine for lung disease flare-ups
articles.content_orig:
Kyle, Texas — Kenney Blewett was diagnosed with lung disease more than a decade ago but started experiencing flare-ups this year that made him feel like he couldn't breathe.
Blewett described those flare-ups as "the scariest thing in the world," said his wife, Cindy, adding that while the episodes typically lasted no more than a few minutes, they had become more frequent.
On top of that, simple tasks, like taking out the trash, left Blewett winded. He rarely left the house and had recently lost 45 pounds. "That sounds like cancer," Cindy remembered one of his doctors said. It was clear, she said, that her husband's poor health, tied to decades of smoking, was getting worse.
That's why, on June 2, Blewett's pulmonologist wrote him a prescription for a new medication to improve the terrifying breathing issues caused by chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or COPD. But the prescription wasn't immediately filled. Two days after that doctor appointment, Blewett received an email from Walgreens explaining that, "due to an insurance issue that we're working to resolve," the medication was delayed.
"He was hopeful that it would work," Cindy said of the drug, two months after her husband's death. "I wish we had the chance to find out."
Insurance delays and denials have become an infamous feature of the American healthcare system, with nearly 7 in 10 adults calling them "a major problem," in a January KFF Health Tracking Poll .
In June 2025, six months after UnitedHealthcare's CEO was shot in New York, the Trump administration announced a highly publicized industry pledge , signed by dozens of major health insurers, to remove some of the barriers that block or delay patients from accessing doctor-recommended care. And yet that pledge was voluntary, and it carries no penalties if companies fail to comply. Indeed, a report published by KFF Health News in July found that some insurers that signed the pledge would not implement all the promised initiatives as originally outlined.
In recent years, lawmakers in most states, including Texas, have attempted to address delays and denials by regulating the insurance industry in the absence of substantial federal reform. But most health insurance plans, including traditional Medicare policies and employer-sponsored offerings, which together cover more than half of all Americans, typically aren't under state jurisdiction.
Even some medical office staff and pharmacy employees find the patchwork of state and federal insurance rules and regulations confusing, a problem that is poised to become more complicated as artificial intelligence plays a larger role in approving and processing claims.
"It's just gotten completely out of hand," said Matt Toresco, CEO of Archō, a patient advocacy and consulting company. He argued that patients need more assistance facing insurance hurdles.
The Blewetts' story illustrates how navigating these complexities remains a herculean task for patients and their caregivers.
Cindy has sought answers from Medicare, Kenney's private Part D drug plan, his pulmonologist's office, and Walgreens. She still has questions about who was responsible for the medication delay and how the holdup could have been prevented.
If the COPD flare-up Blewett experienced on the afternoon of Sunday, June 7, could have been avoided, she wondered, would he still have chosen to die by suicide that night?
During that first week of June, Cindy said her husband repeatedly asked if his prescription — a liquid medication meant to be inhaled through the nebulizer machine Kenney owned — was ready to be picked up from Walgreens.
Cindy said she wasn't initially surprised or worried by the delay. Since its acquisition by a private equity firm last year, Walgreens has cut thousands of jobs across the country, according to the Private Equity Stakeholder Project . Cindy said in August that their Walgreens pharmacy in Kyle seemed to her to have been understaffed for months, and that prescriptions were being filled more slowly.
When Cindy called the pharmacy a few days after Kenney's appointment to find out more about the insurance delay, she said, a Walgreens employee told her the prescription required prior authorization. Also called preapproval or precertification, prior authorization is a practice widely used by health insurers that requires medical providers to seek permission before their patients may receive covered treatment.
But Cindy didn't know which of Kenney's insurers required prior authorization for this medication.
For years, she had helped manage multiple policies on behalf of her husband. Kenney was insured by Medicare Parts A and B, the federal health insurance program for people 65 and older or with disabilities. But he also had a private Part D plan to cover drug costs through Wellcare Value Script, as well as a Medicare supplement plan through Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Texas — also called a "Medigap" plan — that paid for other out-of-pocket costs.
Initially, Cindy assumed that Kenney's Part D plan had invoked prior authorization for his new medication. But because it was a liquid that is inhaled through a nebulizer machine, this drug was one of relatively few covered by Medicare Part B's durable medical equipment benefit , not Part D.
The federal government had no record showing that this prescription had been billed to Kenney's Part B policy, the Medicare agency told Cindy over the phone, she said.
Sarah Tanner and Myriea Amaya, spokespeople for Centene, Wellcare Value Script's parent company, would not answer questions for this article.
After Kenney's death, when Blewett sought clarification at the Walgreens pharmacy, she said the employee "kept saying different things." She recalled his explaining that the prescription was submitted to Medicare Part B but without a necessary diagnostic code that the doctor should have included.
Carmen Lopez, a spokesperson for Walgreens, told KFF Health News in late-September that the company "cannot comment on matters involving specific individuals."
Subsequently, Cindy said, a district pharmacy supervisor for Walgreens reached out by phone, and told her the pharmacy tried to process the prescription through Part B on June 2, the same day as the pulmonologist appointment, but that the prescription was missing a diagnostic code from the physician. The supervisor said Walgreens sent a request for that code to the pulmonologist's office later that day, Cindy recalled.
Kenney's pulmonologist — Rajesh Shetty of LungDocs — did not respond to phone or email messages from KFF Health News. But Cindy said an employee at the practice told her they did not see a fax from Walgreens asking for a diagnostic code for the prescription.
Meanwhile, it couldn't have been an issue with Kenney's Medigap plan, since those policies don't require prior authorization.
"Short of getting attorneys involved," Cindy said, "I'm not sure how to find out what really happened."
Confusion surrounding these Part B and Part D distinctions is common, said Mike Hess, senior director of patient outreach and education at the nonprofit COPD Foundation. "Medicare has gotten to be so complex and convoluted over the years," he said, that even medical office staff and pharmacy employees often misunderstand the nuances.
And with the introduction of AI to the preapproval process, navigating insurance hurdles will likely get more complex for Medicare beneficiaries, doctors say.
Historically, traditional Medicare, unlike Medicare Advantage, used prior authorization sparingly. But in January, Medicare launched a pilot program in six states — Arizona, New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, Texas, and Washington — testing the use of AI to preapprove some healthcare services.
It is intended to "root out waste in Original Medicare," CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz has said, but physicians and patients say the program is creating more red tape for Medicare beneficiaries and leading to inappropriate denials. The pilot program does not current

articles.title_orig: Mount Dora teacher uses social media wish list to feed hundreds of children
articles.title_zh: Mount Dora teacher uses social media wish list to feed hundreds of children
articles.content_orig:
Lisa Bell , Anchor/Reporter
Robert Breuer , Special Projects Producer
MOUNT DORA, Fla. – Meagan DeWitz may not wear a cape, but the Mount Dora teacher is making a powerful difference for children and families across Central Florida.
“I do this because there are so many children who go to bed hungry and wake up hungry,” DeWitz said.
DeWitz is a full-time third-grade teacher and a mother of two. While working at a Title I school, where most students come from low-income households, she saw that the school’s existing food program could not keep up with the demand.
“God put it on my heart,” she said.
So last August, DeWitz launched an organization called Squirrel Around the World. She began by sharing an Amazon wish list on social media, asking people to donate non-perishable food.
The response quickly grew beyond her expectations. Donations began arriving at her home from people across the country - and even from around the world.
“As soon as it comes in, it’s going out,” Dewitz said. “This is an everyday thing - even on the weekends, even on holidays, and even in the summertime, we’re feeding students and it never stops.”
In less than a year, Squirrel Around the World expanded from serving one school to helping 77 schools and organizations across Central Florida.
The need is often greatest for food that does not require refrigeration, a stove or even a kitchen. DeWitz says some families are experiencing homelessness or living in cars and hotels, making shelf-stable food especially important.
“All of our food is non-perishable,” she said. “It could be eaten right out of the package.”
The work can be overwhelming. DeWitz said she has cried in her driveway and carries stories of the families she helps that she does not always share publicly, but the support from what she calls her “squirrel family” keeps her going.
Sabrina Hutchinson, a third-grade teacher at Seminole Springs Elementary, said DeWitz’s work gives teachers peace of mind.
“Teachers, we tend to worry a lot about our kids when they go home,” Hutchinson said. “We know they’re going home and they’re getting dinner, and they are supported with that.”
Demand remains constant. DeWitz said there are times when the nonprofit’s shelves are nearly empty, but donations often arrive just when they are needed most.
“Last week was one of the slowest weeks of the whole year, and I was stressing out so bad because our shelves were empty,” she said. “Then, at the last minute, my squirrel family said, ‘Meagan, relax. We got this.’”
The shelves were soon filled again.
DeWitz hopes to eventually expand Squirrel Around the World beyond Central Florida and help children in communities around the world. For now, she said the nonprofit’s biggest need is not on her food wish list: warehouse space.
To learn more about Squirrel Around the World or find out how to help, visit the organization’s Facebook or TikTok page and Amazon wish list .

articles.title_orig: Trump is bringing big projects to red states. Republicans fear they’re too late.
articles.title_zh: Trump is bringing big projects to red states. Republicans fear they’re too late.
articles.content_orig:
by AMAC — The Association of Mature American Citizens
Photo: Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
With the midterm elections now just over one month away, the mainstream narrative has been that the Trump administration is floundering as Republicans struggle to remain above water in the polls. But despite all the negativity from the press, President Trump has quietly racked up a series of major successes in just the past few weeks that could give a final boost to the GOP heading into Election Day.
Hereâs a look at what you may have missed if you only consumed the mainstream media.
On Monday, Trump announced plans for Mesabi Metallics to construct a massive $15 billion steel mill in eastern Iowa, which the White House says will be the largest steel plant ever built in the United States.
The project is expected to create at least 1,750 permanent jobs while supporting as many as 6,000 construction jobs. Production is slated to begin in 2030 at 7.5 million tons annually, with an eventual capacity of roughly 10 million tons.
The announcement fits squarely within one of Trumpâs signature economic priorities of rebuilding domestic manufacturing and bringing industrial production back to the United States. The steel industry in particular was long treated as a symbol of Americaâs industrial decline. The Iowa project, supplied with iron ore from Mesabiâs new mine in Minnesota, will establish a massive domestic supply chain stretching from mine to mill.
The new plant is also a big win for Republican candidates in tight races in the Hawkeye State this November, particularly the open Senate and gubernatorial races. A huge investment like this gives the GOP a concrete record of success to run on.
On September 29, Trump launched America.gov , which the White House describes as a âsingle digital point of entryâ for accessing federal information and services.
Rather than forcing Americans to navigate a maze of agency websites, the platform uses artificial intelligence drawing on government sources to answer questions and direct users to services.
The current site is only the first phase. Beginning in 2027, the administration says Americans will be able to perform government transactions through the platform, including applying for passports, tracking applications, and updating their names across federal agencies. As just one example, the White House says women who get married will be able to change their name with just a few clicks after uploading the necessary documents.
America.gov promises to ease difficult interactions with government agencies, addressing one of the most persistent frustrations Americans have with Washington.
Trumpâs repeated interest in acquiring Greenland drew plenty of ridicule. But on September 22, Trump joined the leaders of Denmark and Greenland in signing a sweeping Arctic security agreement that dramatically expands Americaâs military position on the strategically vital island.
The agreement allows the United States to expand Pituffik Space Base, establish additional defense areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig, and enjoy extensive military access and overflight rights. It also bars non-NATO countries from establishing military installations or maintaining a persistent military presence in Greenland without agreement from the United States.
In effect, the U.S. now controls Greenland. Trump secured many of his original security objectives, strengthening Americaâs position in an Arctic increasingly contested by Russia and China.
At the United Nations General Assembly on September 22, Trump delivered a powerful defense of his America First foreign policy that will undoubtedly go down as one of the best speeches of his presidency.
âSo, while others have talked, I have acted,â Trump declared , before recounting his administrationâs actions on national security and foreign affairs.
Trump also blasted the U.N. Human Rights Council as âcraven hypocritesâ who âspend their time criticizing the United States for protecting our children from transgender mutilation and transgender insanity and enforcing our immigration lawsâ while ignoring the persecution of Christians and âthe crimes of the worldâs most repressive regimes.â
Trump put the world on notice that America First isnât going anywhere.
On Wednesday, Trump announced plans for $200 billion in South Korean investments in U.S. energy and infrastructure projects, the first major projects emerging from the broader strategic investment package negotiated under last yearâs U.S.-South Korea trade agreement.
The package includes plans involving eight nuclear reactors, a major Texas natural gas power facility, and potentially $54 billion for the long-stalled Alaska LNG project.
Trump highlighted Alaska Senator Dan Sullivanâs support for the LNG project during the Oval Office announcement. If completed, the project would include an 807-mile pipeline carrying North Slope natural gas to an export facility in southern Alaska. That could come up huge for Sullivan as he faces a tough re-election test this year.
The economy added 162,000 jobs in August, the strongest monthly gain since March and more than double the consensus forecast cited by several major outlets. Unemployment remained low at 4.1 percent.
Then on Wednesday, ADP reported that private employers added another 90,000 positions in September, beating economistsâ expectations of roughly 70,000. Manufacturing alone added 17,000 private-sector jobs.
The economy still faces genuine challenges, including elevated energy costs and inflationary pressures. Those problems deserve scrutiny. But so do developments that cut against a uniformly negative picture.
With Election Day approaching, voters will hear plenty about what has gone wrong. But Trump and Republicansâ record also includes major industrial investments, stronger-than-expected hiring, expanded Arctic security arrangements, and an ambitious attempt to modernize federal services. Those successes are part of the national story as well â and deserve to be covered as such.
Shane Harris is the Editor-in-Chief of AMAC Newsline. You can follow him on X @shaneharris513.
