articles.title_orig: Russia Is Planning Its Most Powerful Blow Yet to Try to Freeze Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Russia Is Planning Its Most Powerful Blow Yet to Try to Freeze Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated on September 25 that US President Donald Trump has made a “final decision” to grant Ukraine licenses to produce unspecified types of Patriot air defense systems interceptor missiles. [1] Sources within Zelensky’s administration stated that Ukraine is in negotiations with the United States to obtain licenses for the production of more capable PAC-3 interceptors and the simpler PAC-2 interceptors.[2] Trump himself has yet to confirm his decision to grant Ukraine production licenses for Patriot interceptors as of this writing. Allowing Ukraine to domestically produce Patriot air defense missiles will help improve Ukraine’s ability to more effectively repel Russian ballistic missile strikes, though it will likely take time for Ukraine to establish production facilities and source components necessary to produce interceptors.
Russian forces are intensifying efforts to specifically target Ukrainian data centers and telecommunications infrastructure as part of their ongoing long-range strike campaign aimed at degrading Ukraine’s economy since 2022. Russian long-range strikes have been increasingly targeting Ukrainian internet infrastructure and data centers since mid-September 2026, with the Russian Ministry of Defense (MoD) explicitly mentioning that Russian forces are conducting strikes against data centers and telecommunications infrastructure on September 11.[3] Russian forces have been heavily targeting data centers in Kyiv City every day since September 23, and multiple Ukrainian internet service providers have reported damage to their data centers and subsequent communications disruptions as a result of Russian strikes.[4]
This latest diversification of Russia’s strike campaign aims to disrupt Ukraine’s economy and the digital infrastructure that civilians and businesses rely on daily. Ukrainian officials and business leaders are forecasting that Russia may seek to cause broader telecommunications disruptions that could threaten Ukraine’s banks, online payment providers, businesses, government services, and the military, according to the Financial Times (FT).[5] Ukrainian officials and business leaders added that Russia’s latest strikes against Ukraine’s communications infrastructure, although not a new development in Russia’s full-scale invasion, appear to be a “targeted escalation.” Russia’s strikes since September 23 have caused widespread internet disruptions in Kyiv City.[6] Ukrainian Minister of Foreign Affairs Andriy Sybiha noted that the strikes disrupted Ukrainians’ access to mobile air raid alerts about incoming Russian drones and missiles.[7]
Russian strikes against data centers have reportedly not affected the Ukrainian military, despite the Russian Ministry of Defense claiming that such strikes are meant to degrade the Ukrainian military’s capabilities. The Russian MoD claimed that Russia’s September 11 strikes on data centers aimed to disrupt the Ukrainian military’s network connection.[8] Ukrainian government authorities have not seen indications that Russian strikes damaged the Ukrainian military’s or any state institutions’ communications, however, according to Ukrainian Verkhovna Rada Deputy Oleksandr Fedienko, who heads the Rada Subcommittee on Cybersecurity, Government Communications, and Cryptographic Information Protection.[9]
Russian strikes against data centers and telecommunications infrastructure can cause temporary internet outages but are unlikely to lead to a complete internet shutdown. Ukraine has an extensive network and many internet providers that make a complete shutdown unlikely, according to internet provider representatives speaking to Ukrainian broadcaster Suspilne .[10] Ukrainian Presidential Advisor on Defense Technologies Serhiy “Flash” Beskrestnov stated that Ukraine is unlikely to face a complete internet blackout as the country has some of the most widely distributed internet channels.[11] Russian strikes might, however, lead to increasing internet costs for local users, as internet providers will need to fund repairs to damaged infrastructure.[12]
Russian strikes on data centers are one of the latest Russian attempts to disrupt the Ukrainian economy and follow a similarly targeted Russian strike campaigns against Ukraine’s port and railway infrastructure. Russian forces have recently intensified their strike campaign against Ukraine’s Black Sea port areas, aiming to degrade Ukraine’s ability to use its ports for grain and goods exports as of July 2026.[13] Russian forces are simultaneously targeting Ukrainian railway infrastructure, specifically locomotives, in an effort to disrupt Ukraine’s nationwide railway logistics network.[14] The Kremlin is likely intensifying its strike campaign and diversifying its target sets to seek alternative defeat mechanisms given that Russia’s offensives in 2026 have failed to achieve their objectives, and Ukrainian forces are achieving operationally- and even strategically-significant advances in 2026.[15]
Russian high-ranking military officials continue exaggerating the extent of Russian advances in northern Sumy Oblast as part of the Kremlin’s continuous cognitive warfare effort to portray Ukrainian defenses as collapsing and divert attention from Ukraine’s advances north of Lyman. Russian Defense Minister Andrey Belousov inspected the Russian Northern Grouping of Forces (GoF) on September 25, and the Russian Northern GoF Commander Colonel General Yevgeny Nikiforov claimed that Russian forces seized 10 settlements and over 250 square kilometers in Sumy Oblast over  Summer 2026 and are continuing offensive operations to seize four more settlements in Sumy Oblast.[16] ISW has observed evidence to assess that Russian forces have seized or infiltrated into two settlements and seized or infiltrated into 36.78 square kilometers in Sumy Oblast between June 1, 2026, and August 31, 2026. ISW has also observed evidence to assess that Russian forces seized or infiltrated into eight settlements and seized or infiltrated into 151.66 square kilometers in Sumy Oblast since January 2026, but even those calculations fall short of Colonel General Nikiforov’s exaggerated claims as of September 25. Russian President Vladimir Putin similarly claimed on June 29 that Russian forces advanced up to 10.5 kilometers from Sumy City and later claimed on September 1 that Russian forces were operating 12 kilometers from Sumy City — notably directly discrediting his earlier exaggerated claims.[17] The Russian military has fostered a pervasive culture of lying within its ranks, leading Russian forces to continuously fabricate claims of tactical successes in areas where Russian forces do not maintain enduring positions.[18] Russian military officials have recently claimed false encirclements of Ukrainian forces in northern Kharkiv Oblast and Dobropillya and the Russian MoD’s Sumy Oblast claims are part of Russia’s ongoing cognitive warfare effort to present Russia’s exaggerated battlefield successes in an effort to divert attention from Ukraine’s elimination of the Russian salient north of Lyman in recent months.[19]
We do not report in detail on Russian war crimes because these activities are well-covered in Western media and do not directly affect the military operations we are assessing and forecasting. We will continue to evaluate and report on the effects of these criminal activities on the Ukrainian military and the Ukrainian population and specifically on combat in Ukrainian urban areas. We utterly condemn Russian violations of the laws of armed conflict and the Geneva Conventions and crimes against humanity even though we do not describe them in these reports.

articles.title_orig: 3 Questions: A new resource to empower young entrepreneurs
articles.title_zh: 3 Questions: A new resource to empower young entrepreneurs
articles.content_orig:
Images for download on the MIT News office website are made available to non-commercial entities, press and the general public under a Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial No Derivatives license .
    You may not alter the images provided, other than to crop them to size. A credit line must be used when reproducing images; if one is not provided 
    below, credit the images to "MIT."
The book “Disciplined Entrepreneurship” by Bill Aulet, managing director of the Martin Trust Center for MIT Entrepreneurship and the Ethernet Inventors Professor of the Practice at the MIT Sloan School of Management, walks readers through the 24 steps of starting a venture. With more than half a million copies sold, the approach has proven remarkably effective: MIT students who use the framework in the delta v startup accelerator program have a 61 percent survival/acquisition rate and have collectively raised over $3 billion dollars.
But while the framework is taught at hundreds of colleges around the world, it is not designed for younger students who want to learn about entrepreneurship. To fill that gap, the Trust Center created a free, AI-powered youth entrepreneurship platform called Dear Dreamer , made possible through a gift from the Frank and Eileen Foundation.
Dear Dreamer is open to all students in middle and high school. It adapts the disciplined entrepreneurship framework into a digital, self-paced learning experience featuring short educational videos, interactive exercises, and personalized feedback on the user’s idea. Aulet says the goal is to empower 50,000 young entrepreneurs by 2030.
MIT News spoke with Aulet about the mission of the project and how it came together.
Q: What was the impetus for creating Dear Dreamer?
A: We’ve had a lot of success teaching the disciplined entrepreneurship framework at MIT. Then we made it a course on the online learning platform edX, and we got hundreds of thousands of people taking the class. I used to get emails from people saying, “For the first time in my life, I see myself as an entrepreneur,” or “I see economic security.” At MIT, we often say, “MIT in the world, for the world.” At the Trust Center, we see our mission as, first, train people here at MIT, but also to create more entrepreneurs outside of MIT.
The platform was inspired by the vision of Audrey McLoghlin, the founder and CEO of apparel brand Frank and Eileen and president of the Frank and Eileen Foundation. In my first meeting with Audrey, we were already asking ourselves, “How do we make more entrepreneurs in the world?” I showed her Jetpack, MIT’s generative AI tool trained on disciplined entrepreneurship, which walks MIT students through the entrepreneurial process, and her eyes lit up. She said, “This is how we create more entrepreneurs: We make the work that you guys are doing here accessible to young people.” She wished she had a tool like this when she first started. She also said her daughter wants to be an entrepreneur, but students don’t get much guidance on entrepreneurship at school. MIT has been a great place to keep making this more accessible.
Q: How does the platform work?
A: It takes the core disciplined entrepreneurship curriculum that we know works from our data, and makes it more interactive and engaging for young people. We spent a lot of time working with younger students to figure out how to make it more digestible to a 10-year old, 12-year old, or 14-year old. We put in different case studies and examples for each step of the framework, and we’ve designed the user interface to make it more like Instagram or YouTube, with videos featuring people that students can relate to. But ultimately the content follows the same path we know works; it’s just presented differently from what you would present to an MIT MBA or PhD.
Q: How might learning about entrepreneurship benefit students?
A: Entrepreneurship is a mindset, a skillset, and a way of operating. It allows you to deal with change, and the world’s rate of change is going faster and faster. It’s really not just about founding companies. Founding companies is a great way to learn the mentality that, ‘We can be different. We can build something. We can achieve a lot.’ Someone once said, ‘If you give a person a job, you give them dignity.’ But if you make someone an entrepreneur, it’s like giving them super dignity. They go from a job seeker to a job creator, and they can focus on the things that they’re most interested in, working with the people they want, in the culture they want. We teach students the entrepreneurial mindset and we train them to systematically take an idea and then come up with a solution in an ambiguous, uncertain environment, and iterate on that.
Everyone might not start a company, but even if they go to work at bigger companies, there are a lot of benefits to the entrepreneurial mindset. I’m an entrepreneur now and I’m at MIT, which is not a startup. In a world that’s moving faster and faster, everyone has to deal with change and ambiguity. Starting companies is just a great way to learn. It’s kind of like learning to paint from a blank canvas.
Massachusetts Institute of Technology 77 Massachusetts Avenue, Cambridge, MA, USA

articles.title_orig: AT&T Acknowledges iPhone 18 Pro Max Issues: 'Update Immediately'
articles.title_zh: AT&T Acknowledges iPhone 18 Pro Max Issues: 'Update Immediately'
articles.content_orig:
In a text message sent to customers today, AT&T acknowledged that some iPhone 18 Pro Max devices on its network are experiencing cellular issues .
AT&T said that customers should immediately update to iOS 27.0.1 , despite the fact that many affected users have said that the update does not resolve the issues. There are now at least thousands of users that have experienced this problem, according to discussion topics across the Apple Support Community , Reddit , and MacRumors Forums .
Here is what the text message says:
Hi, it's AT&T. Action needed: An important Apple software update for your iPhone 18 Pro Max is available. Some phones may be unable to complete calls/text/data, including to 911. Update to iOS 27.0.1 immediately — Settings > General > Software Update. Please contact AT&T or Apple if you have questions.
Apple's release notes for iOS 27.0.1 did not mention a fix for AT&T cellular issues. Rather, the update fixed a Face ID issue on the iPhone 18 Pro models.
As we reported last week, affected iPhone 18 Pro Max users are unable to connect to the AT&T network for phone calls, text messages, or data either persistently or intermittently, and their devices typically enter SOS mode as a result. The underlying cause has not been confirmed, and Apple has yet to publicly comment on the matter.
Notably, the U.S. version of the iPhone 18 Pro Max is the only new iPhone unveiled last month that is equipped with a Qualcomm cellular modem . The smaller iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo are equipped with Apple's C2 modem worldwide, as is the iPhone 18 Pro Max in all other countries. However, it is unclear if this is a contributing factor.
If a software issue is identified, then another update such as iOS 27.0.2 may be required. If there is a hardware issue, though, then this would obviously be a much bigger problem. We will provide further updates as new information becomes available.
(P.S. There is some irony in AT&T sending a text message to warn iPhone 18 Pro Max users that they might not be able to send or receive text messages.)

articles.title_orig: The World Needs A Just and Equitable System for AI Governance
articles.title_zh: The World Needs A Just and Equitable System for AI Governance
articles.content_orig:
South-South cooperation provides avenues for countries to extract greater dividends from existing capabilities by pooling resources, sharing implementation lessons and building more context-appropriate AI systems.
The principle of “AI for the positive and for good” undergirds China’s AI+ International Cooperation Initiative, which was unveiled by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of China last September, while the introduction of AI as a formal field of study is generally attributed to a conference held in the summer of 1956, at Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire.
1956 was also the year the world’s first transatlantic undersea telephone cable entered service, connecting Scotland and Newfoundland, Canada. You may also be interested to know that the Chinese Association of Automation was established in 1961. Automation was, and continues to be, an essential area of application for AI.
Today, AI is a global phenomenon. Narratives about AI abound, reflecting the diversity in different countries’ capacity in basic science, technological innovation, business application, regulation and expectations or anxieties about future prospects for AI development. It is possible to summarize the various views as four competing narratives:
1. AI enables and maintains an open and expanding pan-national network of factors of production. In science studies, AI is inherently global. In the social sciences, AI is empowering, but its impact on the pace and direction of change is not uniform. There are major digital gaps between countries and within societies.
2. AI innovation is like an arms race between competing nations. This interpretation is prevalent in public discussions and impacts policy discussions about international cooperation, although mainly among countries with peer-level capacities.
3. AI is an asset in a world market of competing institutions—universities, research labs, funding agencies and the like—and the focus is often on identifying leaders and followers.
4. AI is yet another manifestation of the center-periphery hierarchy in the world system. In this view, some countries are dominant, while others may have to settle for being low on the ladder of digital and associated technologies.
For all countries, AI is an evolutionary product of information and telecommunications technologies, enabling astonishing levels of automation in industrial and service industries.
The marketization of AI models comes in two modalities: closed source and open source. A model is “open” when most of the materials and processes used to create the model are published. When a model is “open weight,” its parameters can be downloaded, run locally, and modified. As such, for users, the difference is not just in the price but also the opportunity for customization. AI models by Chinese companies are open source and open-weight.
Let me try to contrast these models in plain language: With open-source models, you can deploy the model yourself, run it locally or choose a cheaper hosting provider. You do not have to be tied to one company’s pricing or mood. Users juggle in a triangle of choices: affordable, open and good enough. For closed-source models, that is almost impossible.
Still, for many users, especially those in developing countries, a prerequisite for getting on the ladder of AI services is to have in place the enabling infrastructure: a stable supply of quality electricity and locally hosted data centers that allow them to avoid having to compete for the same computing power that serves customers in other countries. For developing countries, the central question is no longer only how to expand digital access but how to turn that access into productive capacity, competitive firms, quality jobs and new trade opportunities.
China’s Belt and Road Initiative, formally launched in 2013, both endorses and promotes efforts to bring digital services to consumers in the Global South. Energy projects by Chinese companies positively contribute to Global South societies’ efforts to move up the energy ladder. Information and communications companies from China bring all devices, networking components, applications and systems that allow people and organizations to interact in the digital world. In the ICT sector, a core feature of Chinese business activities in the Global South is that they offer devices and services at affordable prices to their end users.
With the globalization of the digital economy, cross-border e-commerce has emerged as a new engine for international trade growth and a pathway for developing countries to integrate into global value chains and achieve inclusive development, including for women and minority groups. South-South cooperation, a key mechanism for China and developing countries to pursue collective self-reliance and share the benefits of development, is embracing new opportunities in the digital transformation within the framework of the Global Development Initiative.
The BRI now features all-of-government and all-industry projects grouped into three “Silk Roads”: digital, health and space.
Yes, the space industry is relevant to the pursuit of AI development. For China and the Global South, satellite technologies and services play a vital role in sectors such as agriculture, disaster management and climate monitoring. Despite limited involvement in early space exploration, Global South countries have made significant contributions to space law, advocating for equitable access and the peaceful use of outer space. Many emerging space nations have highly skilled experts in the field of space governance and technology.
A core component of China’s offer to interact with Global South countries is to address the latter’s limited resources to effectively access this expertise available in China. Further cooperation between China and the Global South can, and indeed should, begin with technical training in the dissemination and application of satellite data.
I would be remiss not to mention security concerns associated with the global AI ecosystem. The frameworks being built to evaluate AI systems, the standards being set to govern them and the institutions being created to oversee them have largely been designed for a small set of high-income countries. The Global South—with its diverse languages, institutions and communities— continues to sit at the margins of the larger AI safety discourse.
I proceed from the recognition that moving from insecurity to security is akin to moving from disease to health. In other words, security is relative and relational. There is every reason for Chinese and Global South researchers and entities to approach the issue as one of safety rather than security. Concerns in some parts of the Global South about reliance on foreign-supplied infrastructure, cloud platforms and proprietary models presents a strategic challenge that needs to be put in context: From land stations of undersea cable, to satellite receiving terminals and data centers, every country, large or small, rich or poor, has total sovereign ownership and control. Moreover, AI investments from abroad have to abide by the regulatory rules of a host country in order to function. As such, a Global South country has agency in AI and AI-related foreign investment.
It would be a mistake not to move away from abstract risk taxonomies. If anything, South-South cooperation provides avenues for countries to extract greater dividends from existing capabilities by pooling resources, sharing implementation lessons and building more context-appropriate AI systems.
Chinese President Xi Jinping put it this way at the 2026 World AI Conference and High-Level Meeting on Global AI Governance in Shanghai:
“In China’s view, all countries should take a people-centered approach and develop AI for the positive and for good. We should ensure that AI is a key driver of shared prosperity and common security. We should join hands to build a just and equitable system for global AI governance.”

articles.title_orig: US to send third aircraft carrier towards Iran: US official to Al Jazeera
articles.title_zh: US to send third aircraft carrier towards Iran: US official to Al Jazeera
articles.content_orig:
The United States is deploying a third US aircraft carrier to the waters around Iran, a US official told Al Jazeera, as the war enters its eighth month and both sides weigh escalation and diplomatic engagement.
The official told Al Jazeera that the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group left its San Diego base on Sunday, bound for the region, followed a day later by the Makin Island Marine Expeditionary Force, carrying more than 2,000 Marines.
By the end of November, the official said, three aircraft carriers and two amphibious landing groups will be positioned around Iran.
The official said the concentration of force would hand President Donald Trump a wider menu of options if he decides to act.
Al Jazeera’s Tanya Noury, reporting from Washington, said the new deployment includes thousands of troops and extra air power, including F-35 fighter jets, layered on top of the roughly 50,000 US service members already stationed in the region.
The goal, Noury said, citing sources inside the Pentagon and White House, is to keep military options “on the table” for Trump regardless of how diplomacy unfolds, with the Pentagon not planning to withdraw any assets even if an agreement with Iran is reached. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said forces are “ready to go” should Trump order new strikes.
Trump himself has kept the threat alive in public. He told Fox News he believes the US is “going to win the war” with Iran “very soon”, while suggesting in other remarks that a return to military action “is possible” but something he would rather not spell out before November’s midterm elections.
Washington has paired the show of force with new economic pressure , sanctioning Iran’s rail and automotive conglomerates this week, as the Treasury Department called the new measures an effort to drain what remains of Tehran’s revenue.
Parallel to the military build-up, Iran has pushed a seven-day roadmap , conveyed through Qatar, that would see it reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks in exchange for an end to the US naval blockade, sanctions relief and a regional ceasefire covering Lebanon and Yemen.
The plan was then rejected by Trump.
US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz told NBC the plan’s demand for frozen funds and sanctions relief was non-negotiable, noting “these aren’t just the United States’ sanctions … these are global sanctions”, and pointing to seven UN Security Council resolutions against an Iranian nuclear weapons programme.
Iran’s response, in the meantime, has been similarly two-pronged.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told NBC that Tehran was “fully prepared” to resume the war, before writing on X that “we did not come to New York to sell a war. We came to forge peace.”
Analysts say the mixed signals are deliberate.
Abas Aslani of the Center for Middle East Strategic Studies said the dispute has shifted from whether to negotiate to “who is going to abandon the primary leverage first”, while former US ambassador Richard Schmierer said Trump is caught between delaying past the midterms and the political cost of offering concessions that mirror a June deal he was already criticised for.
Nearly 70 percent of Americans now say the war has not been worth fighting , according to a new AP-NORC poll, with Trump brushing off the slide in his approval ratings by insisting “the pollsters are corrupt”.

articles.title_orig: Campaign-style Trump ads use money meant for border security, memorials
articles.title_zh: Campaign-style Trump ads use money meant for border security, memorials
articles.content_orig:
A GOP senator blocked a resolution on Tuesday that criticized the Trump administration’s recent taxpayer-funded ads promoting President Donald Trump.
Republican Sen. Cynthia Lummis of Wyoming objected to the Democrat-led measure, which stated that taxpayer funds should not have been used for the controversial ads.
The measure, from Democratic Sen. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire, slammed the administration for using government funds for the White House’s recent advertisements. “It is the sense of the Senate that the advertisements promoting President Donald Trump that aired in September 2026, which included the direct language ‘paid for by the U.S. Government,’ should not be paid for by the United States government,” it read.
Senators on both sides of the aisle have criticized the president for using taxpayer dollars for the ads. Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters on Monday, “It’s a great message. I like the message, but it shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars,” and retiring GOP Sen. John Cornyn of Texas added, “no” it’s not appropriate. “It’s not even a close question,” he said.
On the Senate floor on Tuesday, as she introduced her resolution, Hassan said, “The American people want their tax dollars to go towards helping them and keeping them safe, not propaganda campaigns for a president. He’s welcome to run whatever ads he wants with his own riches, but with taxpayer dollars, money that people have worked hard to earn, he needs to follow the law.”
Lummis echoed the White House’s own argument that the ads are comparable to public service announcements released during previous administrations, and are not campaign ads.
“Presidents of both parties have used public service announcements to speak directly to the American people for decades,” the Wyoming Republican said. “The message at the heart of these PSAs is a simple one: American values are worth defending against the failed ideologies of communism and socialism. If that is what has the senator from New Hampshire concerned, I’d suggest the concern says more about her side of the aisle than it does about the PSA.”
One recently released taxpayer-funded television ad features imagery of Trump walking down a hall as audio plays of him saying “this is the final battle.”
“We will cast out the communists, Marxists, and fascists. We will throw off the sick political class that hates our country. We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate America from these villains once and for all,” Trump says in the ad .
Hassan attempted to pass the resolution criticizing the use of taxpayer funding for the ads via a fast-track process known as a unanimous consent request. Any single senator can object to such a request.
President Donald Trump on Wednesday defended the ads, arguing they are not political because he is not on the ballot.
“Well, I’m not running for office, first of all, and so the ads are given by me, but I’m not running for office, and I don’t talk about anybody,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.
The president described the spots as patriotic messaging rather than campaign material. “But when I’m talking about making America great, making our country great, that’s a countrywide ad. That’s an ad for the spirit of our country,” he said.
This story has been updated with additional details.
CNN’s Alejandra Jaramillo contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Boeing engineers, tech workers approve contract, avoid strike
articles.title_zh: Boeing engineers, tech workers approve contract, avoid strike
articles.content_orig:
by Jackie Kent, KOMO News Reporter
SEATTLE — Boeing has avoided an engineering strike after more than 17,000 engineers and technical workers on Thursday approved a four-year contract offer promising wage increases and other perks.
The Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace wrapped up its electronic voting at noon.
PREVIOUS COVERAGE | Boeing releases final contract offer to union engineers, technical workers
The bargaining team had recommended members accept the offer as it guarantees a 34% pay boost over four years, including a nearly immediate 10% increase in October. The deal also enhances health care and retirement benefits and adds two vacation days, a new floating holiday, and three bereavement days.
Alex Phillips is a software security engineer for Boeing in Seattle, and he's been fighting for a big pay bump.
"To improve members’ lives and help Boeing do better," Phillips explained. "There’s a lot of things in this contract that I think are stepping stones for making improvements."
Kevin Boyd works out of the Auburn facility as a cutting tool designer, and said it was critical for this contract to increase base salaries.
"I hope this is a foundation we can continue to build a relationship with Boeing," Boyd added.
The agreement means the aerospace company has narrowly avoided a shutdown of engineering development and regulatory compliance at a time when Boeing is under pressure to improve build quality and clear its aircraft backlog.
"The stakes were really high. Certification of the new Boeing 777 and the [Boeing 737] MAX 10 kind of hung in the balance. Those programs surely would’ve been delayed if the engineers and technicians had gone on strike," Leeham News and Analysis Editor Howard Hardee explained. The trade publication and consulting firm tracks Boeing's production struggles, regulatory hurdles and labor relations.
The machinists went on strike for nearly two months in 2024, which hurt the company's bottom line, brought commercial activity across the Puget Sound area to a standstill and hurt efforts to ramp up production rates for the 737 MAX program. Hardee said that's what Boeing wanted to avoid happening again in this round of negotiations.
"Generally speaking, [Boeing has] had  series of wins. They got the MAX 7 certified," Hardee stated. "They have had a setback on certification of the MAX 10, but getting this negotiation process behind them I think is a really positive development for Boeing, and for people watching the industry it can only be a good sign of their continued recovery."
The company has said these final amounts are $11,000 more for professional employees and $8,000 more for technical workers than under its initial offer, which the union rejected in August.
Following the vote to approve the contract offers, Boeing issued this statement:
“We’re pleased with the outcome of the vote. We look forward to working with our team to support our company’s continued recovery and meeting our customer commitments now and into the future.” – Ben Nimmergut, vice president and functional chief engineer for Production Engineering

articles.title_orig: $1.7 million raised in scheme for Hamas, including from U.S. donors, prosecutors say
articles.title_zh: $1.7 million raised in scheme for Hamas, including from U.S. donors, prosecutors say
articles.content_orig:
Nearly three years after Hamas' Oct. 7 attack on Israel, federal prosecutors allege that more than $1.7 million was funneled to the terrorist group Hamas, including hundreds of thousands of dollars from donors in the United States.
Saleem Alzaq, a 45-year-old Gaza man who prosecutors allege is a longtime Hamas member, was charged with helping operate the fundraising campaign claiming to provide humanitarian aid, according to an indictment unsealed Thursday.
Prosecutors allege Alzaq and his co-conspirators raised funds under the guise of providing food and winter necessities to Palestinians in Gaza between January 2020 and December 2025. The campaigns raised more than $1.7 million, including at least $626,000 from U.S.-based donors, according to the indictment.
Alzaq has been a Hamas member since at least 2017, prosecutors say, and has allegedly posted Hamas propaganda on social media, including posts celebrating the Oct. 7, 2023, attack.
Prosecutors allege Alzaq operated an international fundraising campaign spanning the U.S. and France. Co-conspirators in France allegedly helped collect and transfer money, while two brothers from Louisiana allegedly contributed about $105,000 and a Florida man allegedly provided nearly $50,000 to the terror network.
Alzaq was charged with one count each of conspiring to provide material support to Hamas, conspiring to violate the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, conspiring to commit money laundering and conspiring to defraud the United States. The first three charges each carry a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison if convicted, while the conspiracy to defraud charge carries a maximum of five years. He has not been arrested, and prosecutors say he's been in Gaza during the alleged crimes.
The indictment alleges Alzaq launched a new fundraising campaign on Oct. 7, 2023, that claimed to raise money for Gazans injured that day. The campaign remained open until about Oct. 12 that year, prosecutors said.
Investigators also conducted an undercover operation that prosecutors say provided evidence that Alzaq knew donations were reaching Hamas.
In November 2025, an undercover law enforcement officer posing as a New York-based Hamas supporter contacted Alzaq on Snapchat, according to prosecutors. Alzaq allegedly told the officer he had ways to receive money in New York and offered to connect the officer with contacts there.
The following month, Alzaq allegedly told the undercover officer that he worked with people like the officer who wanted to get money to "the Green," which prosecutors say was a reference to Hamas. He allegedly said he received money and gave it to "the Green," but that it would be difficult to provide proof because Hamas members avoided using identification.
Alzaq also allegedly told the undercover officer that he could deliver money monthly using coded language, including "bread," "bakeries," "buy bread" and "give it to the bakeries."
Prosecutors cited earlier Snapchat messages in which Alzaq allegedly discussed using similar language with a U.S.-based Hamas supporter. After the supporter asked him in January 2024 about money sent to "the bread people," Alzaq allegedly responded that he had "learned the way" and could deliver to them "whatever you want."
The indictment also alleges Alzaq advised donors not to reference Hamas to prevent their accounts from being shut down, including instructing followers in October 2024 not to write "Free Palestine" or "long live Hamas" on donations to his PayPal accounts.
"Our intelligence analysts uncovered this international finance network and built the case that exposed more than $2 million being funneled to Hamas," NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said in a statement. "Saleem Alzaq, a leader in Hamas' military arm responsible for planning and carrying out terrorist attacks, and the other defendants allegedly solicited donations under the guise of humanitarian aid and then directed that money to Hamas."

articles.title_orig: Hochul Names Letitia James as Special Prosecutor in Cornell Case
articles.title_zh: Hochul Names Letitia James as Special Prosecutor in Cornell Case
articles.content_orig:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul has appointed the state's attorney general, Letitia James, as a special prosecutor in investigating the alleged gang rape of a woman at Cornell University.
The woman has alleged she was drugged and raped by several men at a fraternity house. The case, which stems back to 2024, was reopened after the woman filed a civil lawsuit last month that thrust the allegations into the national spotlight.
"New information has raised serious questions about how this case was handled, and I've lost faith in the Tompkins County DA's ability to fairly oversee it," Hochul said.
The announcement means District Attorney Van Houten is no longer overseeing the case.
The BBC has contacted Van Houten's office for comment.
He has defended his office's previous decision not to file charges in the case, arguing they were not given enough evidence to meet the legal threshold.
Van Houten reopened the case after the civil lawsuit and said much of the information released in recent weeks about the case was not passed to his office.
"The young woman at the center of this case deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued," Hochul said in a statement.
James could prosecute any offences that might be found during her investigation and present evidence to a grand jury, Hochul said.
James, who is the state's chief legal officer, said on X that she stood ready "to lead a process guided by the facts and the law".
"The Governor has entrusted my office with this investigation, and we do not take that responsibility lightly," James added.
Hochul and James are scheduled to provide an update on the investigation on Friday morning local time.
The woman at the centre of the case, identified anonymously as Jane Doe in court documents, filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university in September.
Jane Doe is a placeholder name sometimes used in US law for privacy or anonymity reasons.
She alleged that she was drugged and raped by seven men at a fraternity house at the university in 2024.
She claimed that Cornell failed to protect her or adequately punish the men, who have now become known as the Cornell Seven.
The case was initially referred to Van Houten, the top prosecutor in the county, in 2024.
Van Houten said his office did not bring charges at the time because he had only seen a statement from Doe implying the incident was consensual and that she had not been drugged.
This week, his office announced it would be reopening the case - less than two weeks after Doe filed her civil lawsuit.
Cornell has said it provided evidence to the district attorney's office from its own investigation, including a Snapchat group chat in which fraternity members discussed a "free" sexual encounter with Doe on the night of the alleged assault.
Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, has accused the district attorney of repeatedly changing his story amid news coverage of the case.

articles.title_orig: Nike plans job cuts under sweeping restructuring plan
articles.title_zh: Nike plans job cuts under sweeping restructuring plan
articles.content_orig:
Nike on Thursday posted a mixed fiscal first quarter and announced a restructuring plan that will lead to layoffs starting next year.
The company also offered a full-year outlook, saying it expects revenues to decline by a high-single digit percentage in fiscal 2027. Nike also said it expects adjusted earnings per share to be in a range of $1.15 to $1.35.
Shares of Nike fell roughly 3% in extended trading Thursday.
Here's what the company reported for the period compared to what analysts expected, according to consensus estimates from LSEG:
Nike reported net income of $712 million, down 2% from $727 million the year prior.
Revenue fell 4% to $11.21 billion. The retailer said Nike brand revenues took a hit largely due to sustained declines in the China business. Revenue in the market dropped 26%. CEO Elliott Hill said on a call with analysts that the company is "moving with urgency" to improve its business in the region.
Its North America revenue came in at $5.13 billion, just above estimates of $5.11 billion, according to StreetAccount. Nike also reported gross margin of 42.8% compared to estimates of 42.4%.
"Despite that progress, our Nike performance business is not yet large enough to offset the pressure we're seeing in Nike Sportswear, Jordan Brand, and Greater China," Hill told analysts. "We're taking deliberate actions to strengthen those businesses, but realizing the full benefit of those efforts will take time."
Nike's sportswear segment, which Hill said accounted for just under half of the quarter's revenue, fell by a low-double digit percentage.
" Overall, there's a lack of energy in the lifestyle space right now, which is impacting traffic," he said on the call. "Yes, the consumer is cautious, but as the leader in the industry, it's on us to bring more creativity to sportswear."
The sneaker giant also announced a restructuring plan to "position Nike for long-term growth." The strategy is expected to result in layoffs beginning in 2027, though the company did not provide any further details on how many jobs it would cut.
"This work will result in fewer roles across Nike, and I want to acknowledge that news like this creates uncertainty. I don't take that lightly," Hill wrote in a letter to the company.
The cuts are the third round of layoffs Nike has announced this year.
The company said it plans to focus on its supply chain modernization, organizing into three geographies, building a new campus in India and changing its work and workforce. Those geographic regions will be the Americas; the Asia Pacific and Greater China; and Europe, the Middle East and Africa.
The strategy, which Nike has dubbed Pace, is expected to deliver approximately $2.5 billion in savings through fiscal 2031. It'll also result in a 15-cent restructuring expense to fiscal 2027 earnings per share, the company added.
"We expect Pace to streamline decision making, so we can capture demand faster and improve productivity, while also creating greater capacity to invest in what has always set Nike apart: serving athletes, creating industry-leading innovation and building the world's strongest sports brands," Hill said on the conference call.
The retailer has been in the midst of a turnaround plan, focused on improving separate parts of its business at different rates based on priority. The Nike consumer has also been under increased macroeconomic pressure as geopolitical tensions and higher inflation lead to slower spending.
Shares of Nike have plummeted more than 40% this year.

articles.title_orig: FBI arrests Energy Department employee on charge of trying to support Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen
articles.title_zh: FBI arrests Energy Department employee on charge of trying to support Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen
articles.content_orig:
Fox News correspondent Steve Harrigan reports on Iran-backed Houthi rebel gains in the strategic Red Sea region. Hudson Institute senior fellow Rebeccah Heinrichs joins to discuss President Trump urging Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries.
A U.S. Department of Energy worker from Richland, Washington, was arrested Thursday and charged with attempting to provide "material support" to the Iran-backed Houthis, according to the Department of Justice (DOJ).
Ashton Hamed Ellaboudy, 51, is accused of attempting to use his electrical engineering knowledge and background to support the terrorist group in improving its mobile communications infrastructure, secure components for drones as well as chemicals for homemade explosives.
"As alleged, a U.S. government employee traveled overseas and used his specialized expertise in an attempt to aid the Houthis, a designated Foreign Terrorist Organization backed by Iran," Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg said in a statement.
"Additionally, Ellaboudy acquired materials for the construction of explosive material and drones capable of delivering these explosives. These allegations are so deeply disturbing that they almost defy imagination."
IRAN’S PROXY WAR HAS CROSSED OCEANS AND IS NOW KNOCKING ON AMERICA’S DOOR
A Houthi follower during a pro-Iran demonstration in Sanaa, Yemen, April 6, 2026. (Khaled Abdullah/Reuters)
Federal authorities took Ellaboudy into custody after an investigation by the FBI’s Inland Northwest Joint Terrorism Task Force .
According to court records, Ellaboudy first attracted the FBI’s attention after he allegedly bought precursor chemicals, or starting ingredients, and components often used in homemade explosives, as well as parts to make drones .
The DOJ said that, in 2024, Ellaboudy took sick leave from his Department of Energy job and said he had been exposed to highly concentrated nitric acid, a key chemical compound used in explosive manufacturing .
FBI OFFERS $200K REWARD FOR FORMER AIR FORCE INTELLIGENCE AGENT ACCUSED OF SPYING FOR IRAN
Houthi supporters demonstrate in solidarity with Iran during a two-week ceasefire between the U.S. and Iran in Sanaa, Yemen, April 10, 2026. (Khaled Abdullah/Reuters)
In 2025, prosecutors allege, Ellaboudy used an official passport from his previous role with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to travel from Washington state to Oman.
He then crossed into Yemen. After returning to the U.S., Ellaboudy allegedly told border officers his trip was authorized government business.
Investigators also said Ellaboudy advised an undercover FBI confidential human source posing as a representative of a Houthi colonel.
For the Houthis, Ellaboudy allegedly tested solar generators, modified power systems, created circuit schematics and provided support to the group’s communications, the statement said.
NAVY VETERAN AMONG TRIO WHO ALLEGEDLY WANTED TO BEHEAD SOLDIER AND FUND ISIS DRONE ATTACKS ON AMERICANS
The U.S. Department of Energy headquarters June 3, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)
"This individual allegedly betrayed the U.S. and attempted to aid the Houthis, a designated foreign terrorist organization, but thanks to the work of the men and women of the FBI, his actions were detected, and he is now in custody," Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division said.
Officials also confirmed Ellaboudy's alleged activities did not target local nuclear sites.
"This matter did not involve an attempt to harm the Hanford Site or its workforce, and at no time was there a threat to the safety or security of the site," said Ray Geimer, office manager of the Department of Energy Hanford Field Office.
Ellaboudy faces a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison if convicted.

He is scheduled to make his initial court appearance before a federal magistrate judge at 11 a.m. Oct. 2 in Richland, according to the Justice Department.
Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title_orig: Trump launches midterms campaign blitz amid record low approval ratings
articles.title_zh: Trump launches midterms campaign blitz amid record low approval ratings
articles.content_orig:
United States President Donald Trump has kicked off a 32-day campaign tour ahead of the November midterm elections that could see his Republican Party hurt by his handling of the war on Iran and the economy.
On Thursday, Trump travelled from Washington, DC, for back-to-back rallies in Texas and Oklahoma.
At his first stop in Denton, Texas, Trump sought to shift the narrative around his drooping approval ratings, offering a personal assessment of his administration’s performance.
“I give us an A+ on the government, on economics, on everything,” Trump told a crowd of supporters at the Peterbilt Motors Company, a truck manufacturer.
The president also blamed unfair media coverage for his growing unpopularity, arguing that his pre-election rally blitz was necessary to set the record straight.
“We’re doing an extremely poor job of promotion and an extremely great job of running the country,” Trump said.
But Trump’s poll numbers have raised concerns about Republican prospects ahead of the November 3 midterm election.
Trump himself is not on the ballot, but Republican candidates across the country are seeking to defend the right-wing party’s majorities in both chambers of Congress, as well as key state and local offices.
The economy and Trump’s war on Iran are expected to weigh heavily on the election outcome.
On Thursday, The Associated Press and the NORC Center for Public Affairs Research released new poll results showing that 71 percent of Americans disapprove of the war, which has driven up the price of fuel.
About half of survey respondents also said they were worried they would not be able to afford food and petrol. Only 26 percent approved of Trump’s handling of the economy.
Still, despite record low approval ratings, Trump has positioned himself as key to the Republican midterm strategy.
At a first-of-its-kind Republican midterm convention in September, Trump encouraged voters to consider his record while at the ballot box. “I’m asking you to pretend that I’m on the ballot,” he said.
During Thursday’s tour, he touted the impact of his tariff campaign, which he credited with creating thousands of manufacturing jobs.
“For decades, you were heartlessly betrayed by politicians, lousy politicians, who let foreign trade cheaters plunder your wages, loot your factories, close up your jobs,” Trump told Peterbilt workers. “They’d still be doing it if I wasn’t here, believe me.”
Trump’s tariffs, however, have been highly controversial, prompting a series of court challenges. Critics have argued that the sweeping import taxes surpass the president’s constitutional powers.
Trump also used his stump speech to ease concerns about the US-Israel war on Iran, which began on February 28. Both sides have declared victory, though a ceasefire remains elusive.
“Just as I promised, I’m ensuring that Iran will be very quickly ended. I will tell you the energy prices are going to be rapidly, rapidly coming down,” Trump said.
“We’ll win very easily right now,” he added. “I believe right after the election we’ll win, but maybe before the election.”
The war, however, resulted in Iran stopping commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the global fuel trade.
The price of diesel — the fuel the trucks built at the plant use — soared to record highs of more than $6 per gallon (3.8 litres) last week. Petrol prices have similarly skyrocketed.
Trump, however, has acknowledged that the stakes are high for his presidency in the upcoming midterms.
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are up for grabs, as are 35 seats in the 100-member Senate.
Losing Republican control of either chamber could create roadblocks for Trump’s legislative agenda during the final two years of his second term.
But Trump has also expressed concern that he could be impeached for a third time, after two prior impeachments during his first presidency.
At Thursday’s second stop, in Durant, Oklahoma, the Republican leader repeated that fear. “Pretend I’m running, please,” he told the crowd. “If we don’t win, they’ll end up impeaching me.”
Many of the places Trump is scheduled to visit this month are perceived as reliably Republican voting districts. Following his stops in Texas and Oklahoma on Thursday, Trump will be heading to Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska in the coming days.
Still, some elections that ordinarily would be considered shoo-ins for Republicans have grown more competitive in recent months.
In Texas, for instance, no Democrat has won a statewide race since the 1990s. But this year, Republican Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general, is struggling to win a Senate contest against Democrat James Talarico.
During both of Thursday’s stops, Trump sought to bolster Paxton’s prospects. At the Peterbilt factory, for instance, he called Paxton “the greatest attorney general in the United States of America”.
“We gotta get this guy elected,” Trump said, before pivoting to criticisms of Talarico, whom Republicans have sought to paint as out of touch with Texas’s large beef industry.
“He’s a vegan,” Trump said of Talarico, repeating an unsubstantiated rumour. “And vegans don’t do well in Texas.”
But leaked audio appeared to show Paxton lamenting the negative impact Trump had by holding the Republican midterm convention in Texas last month.
“It dropped our numbers. Everybody’s numbers dropped,” Paxton reportedly said.
Trump has nevertheless used his pre-election tour to highlight social issues he feels will help rally voters to the Republican cause.
On Thursday, he returned to familiar subjects like immigration and transgender rights, which he depicted as a part of the Democrats’ “radical” agenda.
“They want women in men’s sports. They want open borders. They want transgender mutilation for your children,” Trump said. “What the hell are you thinking about, you liberals?”
The president also used his Texas appearance to push back against critics of data centres, despite bipartisan concern .
Critics worry that the rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) has fuelled the proliferation of data centres, which require large amounts of electricity and water to process mass data quantities.
While Trump has dismissed fears about AI as largely unfounded, a poll last month found 53 percent of Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about the technology’s environmental impacts.
Even fellow Republicans in Texas are responding to public pressure about the growing number of data centres, more than 300 of which are operational, with hundreds more in progress.
In August, Governor Greg Abbott called for an audit of all data centres to map their water and electricity usage, and the following month, Paxton in his role as state attorney general launched an investigation into whether they were complying with water reporting requirements.
Trump nevertheless used his Texas rally to tout the expansion of such enterprises.
“It’s a huge thing. It’s bigger than the industrial revolution,” he said, dismissing the concerns as part of a “scam”. He then explained he had urged AI companies to “take care of the people”.
“They’re making a fortune for the communities,” he added.

articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump announced U.S. troops will leave Iraq by the end of September, ending a 23-year presence.
The U.S. military has completed the withdrawal of American forces and equipment from Erbil Air Base in Iraq, ending its Operation Inherent Resolve mission, U.S. Central Command announced Wednesday.
The departure closes the Iraq chapter of the U.S.-led military mission launched against ISIS in 2014, while shifting primary responsibility for the country's security to Iraqi forces. The broader counter-ISIS campaign is not ending, however, with the U.S.-led task force relocating its headquarters to Jordan and operations continuing in Syria .
"Job well done to the tens of thousands of American service members, diplomats, and civilian personnel who answered the call in Iraq," CENTCOM Commander Admiral Brad Cooper said.
US SERVICE MEMBER KILLED IN IRAQ AS TROOPS RECOVER UNIDENTIFIED REMAINS IN JORDAN: CENTCOM
Soldiers from the U.S.-led coalition forces are seen during the handover of the K1 Air Base to the Iraqi Army from the U.S.-led coalition in Kirkuk, Iraq on March 29, 2020. (The Associated Press)
"Because of your grit, sacrifice and professionalism, ISIS no longer poses a systemic threat to Iraq’s national security and Iraqi security forces, including the Peshmerga and other Iraqi Kurdistan Region security forces, now possess the capacity, leadership, and operational independence to unilaterally manage threats to their homeland," Cooper said.
Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell called the departure the formal conclusion of Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq and said it marked a transition "from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship."
MOTORCYCLE PATROLS IRANIAN CITIES, CHECKPOINTS RISE AS REGIME BRACES FOR UNREST
The Pentagon said the U.S. will continue providing targeted training and intelligence support to Iraqi forces even after the withdrawal, while Iraqi security forces, including the Peshmerga, take the lead in keeping ISIS remnants suppressed.
Erbil Air Base in northern Iraq served as the main operational hub for Combined Joint Task Force — Operation Inherent Resolve and hosted most of the roughly 1,500 American and coalition forces supporting counter-ISIS operations , according to CENTCOM.
U.S. and coalition forces began leaving federal Iraq last October as Washington and Baghdad moved toward a bilateral defense relationship. The final removal of personnel and equipment from Erbil completed that transition on Sept. 30. The withdrawal followed an agreement reached between Washington and Baghdad under the Biden administration in 2024 and carried forward under the Trump administration.
Admiral Charles Bradford "Brad" Cooper II, commander of U.S. Central Command, speaks during a joint press conference at CENTCOM headquarters at MacDill Air Force Base in Tampa, Florida, on March 5, 2026. (Octavio Jones/AFP via Getty Images)
Combined Joint Task Force — Operation Inherent Resolve remains active and is now headquartered in Jordan, according to CENTCOM. U.S. forces also continue counter-ISIS operations in Syria alongside coalition partners and the Syrian government.
SYRIA OFF US TERROR BLACKLIST AFTER NEARLY 50 YEARS AS TRUMP ADMIN CLEARS INVESTMENT HURDLE
The U.S. has roughly 4,000 troops stationed in Jordan, where American forces will continue monitoring the ISIS threat. Muwaffaq Salti Air Base hosts U.S. combat aircraft and has itself become a target during the conflict with Iran. Three U.S. service members were killed in an Iranian attack on the base in July.
"As we step back and hand full primary responsibility for Iraq’s security to the Government of Iraq and the brave people of Iraq, U.S. and coalition forces stationed across the region will remain ready to respond to any ISIS threats that arise," Cooper said.
"Maintaining our vigilance and readiness is essential to protecting the U.S. homeland and strengthening regional security," he added.
The withdrawal ends a U.S. military presence in Iraq that was reestablished in 2014, when Iraqi authorities sought international assistance as ISIS captured large areas of the country. U.S. troops had previously left Iraq in 2011 following the 2003 invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein.
With U.S. forces leaving by Sept. 30 and as Baghdad tries to rein in Iran-backed militias, Iraq could also be entering its most dangerous period since ISIS seized Mosul in 2014. (REUTERS/Mohammed Ameen)
For the last several years, roughly 2,500 U.S. troops have been stationed in Iraq. The majority departed last year, leaving hundreds of troops in the northern Kurdish region until the final withdrawal.
The final departure comes as Iraq faces a separate security challenge from powerful Iran-backed militias operating inside the country. Baghdad has sought to bring weapons held by non-state groups under government control, but some of the most influential militias have resisted disarming.
IRANIAN PRESIDENT BLAMES US FOR MIDDLE EAST CONFLICT WHILE DENYING NUCLEAR AMBITIONS, OFFERS TO DILUTE URANIUM
The Pentagon explicitly identified those militias as one of the security challenges Baghdad will now be expected to confront.
"The primary responsibility for addressing Iraq's remaining security challenges, including ISIS remnants and Iran-aligned militias that undermine Iraqi sovereignty and regional stability, now rests with the Government of Iraq," Parnell said.
The withdrawal also reduces the number of U.S. military targets inside Iraq after American forces there faced repeated attacks by Iran-aligned groups following Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel. During this year's war with Iran, seven of the 18 U.S. service members killed in Iranian attacks were killed in Iraq, according to Fox News reporting.
The withdrawal has drawn sharply different reactions inside Iraq. Iran-aligned groups celebrated the U.S. departure, while officials in the country's Kurdish region have raised concerns about the loss of American air-defense capabilities amid drone and missile threats.
Kurdish officials say their region has faced more than 1,000 Iranian drone and ballistic missile attacks since the war with Iran began Feb. 28, adding to concerns over the removal of U.S. forces and air-defense capabilities.
Thousands of ISIS fighters also remain in Iraq and Syria despite the collapse of the terror group's organized military threat. The Iraqi government has said its forces will continue operations against ISIS, while the Pentagon said the U.S. remains committed to preventing the group from reconstituting from Iraqi territory.

CENTCOM said U.S. and coalition forces elsewhere in the region will remain prepared to respond if ISIS again poses a threat.
"The United States supports a strong sovereign Iraq that secures its borders, protects its people, and serves as the foundation for deeper commercial, diplomatic, and security cooperation between our two countries," Parnell said.

articles.title_orig: Alleged Hamas fundraiser to undercover agent: I have a network in New York
articles.title_zh: Alleged Hamas fundraiser to undercover agent: I have a network in New York
articles.content_orig:
Nearly three years after Hamas' Oct. 7 attack on Israel, federal prosecutors allege that more than $1.7 million was funneled to the terrorist group Hamas, including hundreds of thousands of dollars from donors in the United States.
Saleem Alzaq, a 45-year-old Gaza man who prosecutors allege is a longtime Hamas member, was charged with helping operate the fundraising campaign claiming to provide humanitarian aid, according to an indictment unsealed Thursday.
Prosecutors allege Alzaq and his co-conspirators raised funds under the guise of providing food and winter necessities to Palestinians in Gaza between January 2020 and December 2025. The campaigns raised more than $1.7 million, including at least $626,000 from U.S.-based donors, according to the indictment.
Alzaq has been a Hamas member since at least 2017, prosecutors say, and has allegedly posted Hamas propaganda on social media, including posts celebrating the Oct. 7, 2023, attack.
Prosecutors allege Alzaq operated an international fundraising campaign spanning the U.S. and France. Co-conspirators in France allegedly helped collect and transfer money, while two brothers from Louisiana allegedly contributed about $105,000 and a Florida man allegedly provided nearly $50,000 to the terror network.
Alzaq was charged with one count each of conspiring to provide material support to Hamas, conspiring to violate the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, conspiring to commit money laundering and conspiring to defraud the United States. The first three charges each carry a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison if convicted, while the conspiracy to defraud charge carries a maximum of five years. He has not been arrested, and prosecutors say he's been in Gaza during the alleged crimes.
The indictment alleges Alzaq launched a new fundraising campaign on Oct. 7, 2023, that claimed to raise money for Gazans injured that day. The campaign remained open until about Oct. 12 that year, prosecutors said.
Investigators also conducted an undercover operation that prosecutors say provided evidence that Alzaq knew donations were reaching Hamas.
In November 2025, an undercover law enforcement officer posing as a New York-based Hamas supporter contacted Alzaq on Snapchat, according to prosecutors. Alzaq allegedly told the officer he had ways to receive money in New York and offered to connect the officer with contacts there.
The following month, Alzaq allegedly told the undercover officer that he worked with people like the officer who wanted to get money to "the Green," which prosecutors say was a reference to Hamas. He allegedly said he received money and gave it to "the Green," but that it would be difficult to provide proof because Hamas members avoided using identification.
Alzaq also allegedly told the undercover officer that he could deliver money monthly using coded language, including "bread," "bakeries," "buy bread" and "give it to the bakeries."
Prosecutors cited earlier Snapchat messages in which Alzaq allegedly discussed using similar language with a U.S.-based Hamas supporter. After the supporter asked him in January 2024 about money sent to "the bread people," Alzaq allegedly responded that he had "learned the way" and could deliver to them "whatever you want."
The indictment also alleges Alzaq advised donors not to reference Hamas to prevent their accounts from being shut down, including instructing followers in October 2024 not to write "Free Palestine" or "long live Hamas" on donations to his PayPal accounts.
"Our intelligence analysts uncovered this international finance network and built the case that exposed more than $2 million being funneled to Hamas," NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said in a statement. "Saleem Alzaq, a leader in Hamas' military arm responsible for planning and carrying out terrorist attacks, and the other defendants allegedly solicited donations under the guise of humanitarian aid and then directed that money to Hamas."

articles.title_orig: Renée Good’s family sues Trump officials, saying death was ‘not an accident’
articles.title_zh: Renée Good’s family sues Trump officials, saying death was ‘not an accident’
articles.content_orig:
The partner of Renee Good, a Minneapolis woman who was fatally shot by an immigration officer in January , spoke publicly about her death for the first time Thursday as the family announced that they have filed two federal civil lawsuits.
“She was pure love, and she was funny, and she was smart, and she was gorgeous,” Becca Good said at a news conference, becoming emotional as she discussed attending back-to-school night and preparing to celebrate Halloween with their children alone.
“Every single one of these moments for all of her babies and for everyone up here was a monumental moment, and she should be here for all of them. We were all robbed,” she said.
Earlier in the news conference, attorneys for Renee Good’s family announced lawsuits alleging wrongful death and excessive force in her Jan. 7 death.
One lawsuit seeks to hold the United States liable under the Federal Tort Claims Act for the actions of federal agents. It alleges wrongful death, battery, assault, false imprisonment, emotional distress and negligence.
The second suit names Jonathan Ross, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who shot Good, as well as several federal officials, including White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller and former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem.
“Every morning she’s my first thought. I think about how the kids are growing up without their mama and how I’ll grow old without the love of my life,” Becca Good said.
Renee Good’s brother, Brent Ganger, said her death was “completely senseless.”
“We file these two lawsuits today to put officials on notice that we have not forgotten,” he said.
The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to requests for comment. A representative for Ross could not immediately be identified.
White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said the office will “vigorously defend” the claims in the lawsuits. Bis also shared a statement from President Donald Trump, who said Good’s “actions were pretty tough.”
“When you look at the way that car was pulled away ... there are a couple versions of that tape that are very very bad,” Trump said.
Good, 37, was fatally shot in the driver’s seat of her SUV during a Jan. 7 encounter with Ross. The killing occurred about a month after the Trump administration deployed 3,000 immigration agents to the Twin Cities in what officials have dubbed Operation Metro Surge. Agents descended on Minnesota after right-wing influencers drew attention to a state fraud scandal involving Somali nationals.
The operation triggered massive protests and significant pushback from state leaders. It ended in February .
The shooting was captured on cellphone video. It showed Good’s partner, Becca Good , standing outside the SUV calling Ross “big boy” and telling him to remove the covering from his face. Other officers at the scene could be heard telling Good to get out of the car. In the video, Good is seen turning the steering wheel away from Ross and beginning to drive.
Multiple gunshots can be heard in the video before Good’s SUV crashes into a parked car. In a separate video recorded by Ross, a male voice could be heard saying “f-----g b----” moments before the crash.
Trump administration figures, including President Donald Trump and Noem, defended Ross’ actions and claimed Good was an agitator who tried to run over the officer with her vehicle. Witnesses told NBC News at the time that Ross didn’t appear to be in the direct path of the SUV.
Noem said Ross was treated at a hospital for injuries he sustained in the incident and was released soon after. A DHS official previously told NBC News that Ross sustained internal bleeding but did not elaborate on his injuries.
Attorney Antonio M. Romanucci, who is representing Good’s family, said he hopes the lawsuits “are the beginning of the ultimate legal weapon in uncovering the truth behind this unlawful use of deadly force and the nefarious conspiracies behind the invasion of American cities by American law enforcement officers.”
Weeks after Good’s killing, Customs and Border Protection agents shot and killed Alex Pretti , a 37-year-old intensive care nurse, in Minneapolis.
Minyvonne Burke is a senior breaking news reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_zh: Online claims revive mercury mystery around tomb of first Chinese emperor

A Weibo hashtag about ancient cinnabar sites has reignited debate over the ‘rivers and seas’ in Qin Shi Huang’s mausoleum
Online claims that archaeologists have identified the source of mercury in the mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang – China’s first emperor, who unified the country more than 2,000 years ago – have revived interest in ancient cinnabar sites in northwestern China’s Shaanxi province.
The claims, which sent related hashtags trending on social media late last month, centred on three sites in Xunyang where archaeologists last year found evidence of cinnabar mining, processing and transport during the pre-Qin and Qin-Han periods.

articles.title_orig: Lacey Kindel, Sam Powell named to Canada squad for U17 World Cup
articles.title_zh: Lacey Kindel, Sam Powell named to Canada squad for U17 World Cup
articles.content_orig:
Michigan State Fr. M, Lacey Kindel (10), crosses the ball towards the net for her teammates in DeMartin Stadium in East Lansing, Mich., on Aug. 12, 2026.
No. 2 Michigan State Women’s Soccer freshman midfielder Lacey Kindel and freshman goalkeeper Sam Powell were named to the Canada squad for the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup later this month.
The pair will travel to Morocco for the tournament that will take place from Oct. 17 to Nov. 7.
Kindel scored her first goal on Sunday and has played significant minutes off the bench throughout the season. Powell has not yet touched the field for the Spartans. Both are 17, some of the youngest players in the NCAA.
Kindel is one of four players on Canada’s roster playing in their second World Cup. She competed for Canada in both the 2024 U-15 CONCACAF Championship, where Canada won bronze, and the 2025 FIFA U-17 Qualifiers and World Cup in Morocco in October, where Canada advanced to the quarterfinals. She started four of five games at the World Cup last year.
Kindel scored four goals in three games to help Canada qualify. She was named to the Women’s U-17 Qualifiers Best XI by CONCACAF. She is a frequent captain of the side.
It will be Powell’s first World Cup, but not her first experience for Canada. She earned a call-up to the Canadian Women’s National U-17 squad for the 2025 Four Nations Cup and won a bronze medal at the 2024 U-15 CONCACAF Championship alongside Kindel.
Kindel, from Vancouver, British Columbia, and Powell, from Winnipeg, Manitoba, have a long history of playing together. Both came through the Vancouver Rise Academy, where Kindel became the youngest player ever in Canada’s top division, and Powell became the youngest keeper to play in the CONCACAF W Cup in both 2024 and 2025.
Canada will compete in Group C against Brazil, Norway and Ghana. The tournament kicks off for Canada on Oct. 18 against Brazil.

articles.title_orig: World premiere of ʻAinakea opens Friday at Historic ʻĪao Theater
articles.title_zh: World premiere of ʻAinakea opens Friday at Historic ʻĪao Theater
articles.content_orig:
Privacy Policy | About Our Ads
Maui OnStage will present the world premiere of ʻAinakea.  PC: courtesy
Maui OnStage will present the world premiere of ʻAinakea , a new play by Maui playwright James Nevius, opening Friday, October 2, at the Historic ʻĪao Theater. Set in West Maui in 1953, the play explores a family, a plantation and an island on the cusp of profound change.
Hawaiʻi is still a territory, the plantation economy is shifting, and the Goodale family—descendants of early missionaries and longtime owners of the sugar plantation ʻAinakea—is running out of money. As family, friends and plantation workers gather to confront the future of the estate, a larger question emerges: Who should be the stewards of the land?
Inspired by Anton Chekhov’s The Cherry Orchard , ʻAinakea brings that classic story of a changing social order into a distinctly Maui setting, exploring labor, family, Hawaiian identity, memory and the changing island.
“This is a story about a particular place and a particular moment in Maui’s history, but the questions it raises are much bigger,” said Luana Whitford-Mitchell, Executive Director of Maui OnStage. “What happens when the world we know begins to change? And who gets to decide what happens to the land? We’re excited to bring James Nevius’ work to the stage for its world premiere.”
Directed by Francis Tauʻa, ʻAinakea features a Maui cast and creative team whose work creates a strong sense of time and place.
Scenic Designer Amanda Dellinger’s set takes its inspiration from the Hanakaʻōʻō ahupuaʻa (land division) located in the moku (district) of Kāʻanapali, including a backdrop based on the silhouette of the West Maui mountain range above the former Puʻukoliʻi Village camp. She also honors the memory of two historic Lahaina buildings lost in the wildfires by incorporating three colors from Ameritone-Maui’s Lahaina Restoration Foundation historic color palette.
Costume Designer Sarah Loney Mark combines true vintage and vintage-inspired pieces to evoke 1953 Maui. Vince Pinelli’s evocative lighting and the collaborative atmospheric sound design of Dawn Harper and Sam Castillo further immerse audiences in the world of ʻAinakea .
Audiences will have an opportunity to hear directly from James Nevius during Talk Story with the Playwright , held immediately following the Sunday performances on Oct. 4 and Oct. 11 .
What: ʻAinakea — World Premiere When: Oct. 2–18, 2026 Performances: Fridays at 7:30 p.m.; Saturdays and Sundays at 3 p.m. Were: Historic ʻĪao Theater, 68 N. Market Street, Wailuku Tickets: $10–$45 Tickets and Information: MauiOnStage.com | 808-242-6969
Maui OnStage extends a special mahalo to its 2026 Season Sponsor, Wave of Harmony Foundation in partnership with Marji Knowles and Michael Tibbott .
Maui OnStage is Maui’s community theater company, presenting live theater and educational performing arts experiences at the historic ʻĪao Theater in Wailuku. Founded in 1931, Maui OnStage has been part of Maui’s performing arts community for more than nine decades.
